title: How a new person begins: egg cell, sperm cell, the first week, and families of many kinds

summary.text: Only one sperm cell joins the egg cell. So why do many millions set out? In this lesson you will run the Two Gates Test with beans and a die to find out. You will learn where egg cells and sperm cells are made, how they meet, and what happens in the first week. You will also learn how bodies get ready at puberty, how doctors can help a baby begin, and the many ways families are made.
summary.art: A large pale round egg cell with a single tiny sperm cell touching the edge, and far behind, a long fading trail of thousands of other tiny sperm cells that did not arrive.

intro.hook: You began as one cell, smaller than a grain of salt. That cell was made when two cells joined: one egg cell and one sperm cell. Only one sperm cell was needed. Yet many millions of sperm cells set out. Why so many? Say what you think, and say why.
intro.text: Most people guess that the sperm cells are racing, and the fastest one wins. That is not what scientists find. You will first make the egg cell and the sperm cell at a size you can see. Then you will run a test with beans and a die, and your own numbers will show why so many must start. After that you will follow the two cells from where they are made to where they meet, and through the first week of a new person.
intro.art: A child at a table looking closely at one grain of salt on a sheet of dark paper, with a steel plate and a grain of rice with a thread tail beside it.

outcomes: I can say what an egg cell and a sperm cell are, where each is made, and how they differ.
I can explain what fertilisation is, and why the egg cell and the sperm cell each carry half the instructions.
I can describe how sperm cells reach the egg cell, and what happens in the first week, until the embryo attaches in the womb.
I can use a model and my own results to explain why millions of sperm cells start when only one joins the egg cell.
I can explain how XX or XY is settled, and why nobody chooses it.
I can describe how bodies change at puberty, and say what a period is.
I can name several ways a family is made, including IVF and adoption.
I can say what is still unknown about how a baby begins, and tell a model from the real thing.

terms.meaning: An egg cell is the cell from a woman's body that can join with a sperm cell to start a baby. It carries half of the instructions for a new person, and a store of food and working parts.
terms.example: A human egg cell is about one tenth of a millimetre across. That is about a third of the width of a grain of table salt.
terms.art: A round pale cell wrapped in a clear coat, drawn beside a grain of salt three times as wide.

terms.meaning: A sperm cell is the cell from a man's body that can join with an egg cell. They have a small head, which carries half of the instructions, and a long tail for swimming.
terms.example: A sperm cell is about one twentieth of a millimetre long. Twenty of them, end to end, would measure one millimetre.
terms.art: A tiny cell with an oval head and a long thin wavy tail, swimming to the right.

terms.meaning: An ovary is one of two small organs in a woman's lower belly where egg cells are kept and ripened. Each is about the size of an almond in its shell.
terms.example: A baby girl is born with all her egg cells already in her two ovaries.
terms.art: A simple outline of a woman's lower belly showing two small oval ovaries, one on each side of the womb.

terms.meaning: A testis is one of two oval organs where a man's body makes sperm cells. The two testes hang outside the belly, in a pouch of skin called the scrotum.
terms.example: The testes stay about 2 degrees cooler than the inside of the body. Sperm cells are made best at that cooler temperature.
terms.art: A simple side outline of a man's lower body with the two testes in the scrotum labelled, drawn as a plain diagram.

terms.meaning: The womb is a hollow organ of strong muscle in a woman's lower belly, where a baby grows before birth. Doctors call it the uterus.
terms.example: An empty womb is about the size of a small pear. It stretches to hold a baby, the placenta and the water around the baby.
terms.art: A pear-shaped hollow organ with a thick muscle wall and a soft inner lining coloured pink.

terms.meaning: An egg tube is a thin tube, about as long as your hand is wide, that leads from near an ovary to the womb. There are two. Doctors call them fallopian tubes.
terms.example: The egg cell and the sperm cell meet inside an egg tube, not inside the womb.
terms.art: A womb with two thin tubes curving out from its top corners, each ending in soft fringes beside an ovary.

terms.meaning: Ovulation is when a ripe egg cell leaves the ovary. In most women it happens about once a month.
terms.example: After ovulation the egg cell can be fertilised for only about one day.
terms.art: A ripe egg cell leaving the surface of an ovary, with the fringes of an egg tube close by.

terms.meaning: A chromosome is one long thread of DNA, wound up tightly. DNA is the chemical that holds the instructions for building a body.
terms.example: Most cells in your body have 46 chromosomes. An egg cell has 23, and a sperm cell has 23.
terms.art: Twenty-three pairs of small X-shaped threads set out in rows, with the last pair circled.

terms.meaning: Fertilisation is when a sperm cell joins with an egg cell, and their two half-sets of chromosomes come together in one cell.
terms.example: In humans, fertilisation happens in an egg tube, usually within a day of ovulation.
terms.art: One sperm cell with their head inside the coat of a large round egg cell, and other sperm cells left outside.

terms.meaning: A zygote is the single cell made by fertilisation. It has a full set of 46 chromosomes, 23 from the egg cell and 23 from the sperm cell.
terms.example: You were a zygote for about one day. Then you divided into two cells.
terms.art: One round cell with two small round shapes inside, moving towards each other.

terms.meaning: An embryo is a new living being in the earliest stages of growing. In humans the name is used from the first cell divisions to the end of week 8.
terms.example: On about day 5, a human embryo is a hollow ball of about 100 to 200 cells.
terms.art: A hollow ball of cells with a small clump of cells on the inside at one end.

terms.meaning: Implantation is when the embryo attaches to the soft lining of the womb and begins to grow into it.
terms.example: Implantation usually happens 8 to 10 days after ovulation. Until then the embryo is floating free.
terms.art: A tiny hollow ball of cells sinking into a thick, soft pink lining.

terms.meaning: Puberty is the time when a child's body slowly changes into an adult's body, and becomes able to make a baby one day.
terms.example: Puberty usually begins between 8 and 13 in girls and between 9 and 14 in boys. It takes several years.
terms.art: A height chart on a wall showing a child at three ages, growing taller, with a calendar beside it.

terms.meaning: A hormone is a chemical message that one part of the body makes and the blood carries to other parts.
terms.example: At puberty, a small gland under the brain sends hormones to the ovaries or the testes, and they start their adult work.
terms.art: A small gland under the brain with dotted arrows running down through the blood to the lower belly.

terms.meaning: A period is a few days each month when the lining of the womb comes away and leaves through the vagina as blood. It is a healthy part of the monthly cycle.
terms.example: Each month the womb builds a soft lining. If no embryo arrives, the lining is not needed, and the body lets it go.
terms.art: A paper calendar for one month with five days at the start shaded red and one day in the middle marked with a small circle.

terms.meaning: IVF is a way doctors help a baby begin. The egg cell and the sperm cells are brought together in a dish, and the embryo is then placed in the womb. The letters stand for in vitro fertilisation, which means fertilisation in glass.
terms.example: The first baby born after IVF was Louise Brown, in England in 1978. The second was Durga, in Kolkata, 70 days later.
terms.art: A woman scientist in a white coat looking down a microscope at a small round glass dish.

terms.meaning: Adoption is when grown-ups become the parents of a child who was born to someone else. It is done by law, and it is for life.
terms.example: An adopted child began from an egg cell and a sperm cell like everyone else. Their parents are the people who raise them.
terms.art: Two adults and a child sitting together on a mat, sharing a meal from steel plates and laughing.

terms.meaning: Mitochondria are tiny parts inside a cell that release energy from food. They carry a small piece of DNA of their own.
terms.example: All your mitochondria came from the egg cell. So they came from your mother, and from her mother before her.
terms.art: A cell cut open to show several small bean-shaped parts with folded insides, and a small ring of DNA drawn in one of them.

explanations.concept: Two kinds of cell can start a new person: the egg cell and the sperm cell
explanations.definition: An egg cell and a sperm cell are sex cells. Each carries half of the instructions for a person. When one of each joins, a new person can begin.
explanations.description: Almost every cell in your body can only make more cells of the same kind. A skin cell makes skin cells. Two kinds of cell are different. An egg cell is large for a cell, about a tenth of a millimetre across. You could just see one as a speck. A sperm cell is far smaller, with a tail for swimming. Why are they so different? They have different work. The egg cell stays in place, and brings the food and the working parts that the new cell needs for the first days. The sperm cell has to travel, so they carry almost nothing but the instructions, a tail, and mitochondria to power the tail. Neither cell can grow into a baby alone. In humans and other mammals, an embryo needs instructions from both. Sex cells are alive. They sense chemicals around them and respond.
examples: If an egg cell were as big as a steel dinner plate, a sperm cell would be a grain of rice with a tail about as long as your finger.
A hen's egg yolk also begins as one egg cell. It is huge because the chick grows outside the mother, so all the food must be packed in first.
A human embryo is fed through the placenta. So a human egg cell needs to carry food for only the first week or so.
explanations.art: A large round egg cell and, at the same scale, a tiny sperm cell with a long tail, with a ruler mark showing one tenth of a millimetre.

explanations.concept: Half and half: why each sex cell carries 23 chromosomes
explanations.definition: Most body cells have 46 chromosomes, in 23 pairs. An egg cell or a sperm cell has only 23, one from each pair.
explanations.description: Suppose egg cells and sperm cells had 46 chromosomes each. Then the first cell of a baby would have 92. That baby's own children would have 184. The number would double in every generation, and cells cannot work like that. So when a body makes sex cells, the cells divide in a special way that halves the number. This kind of division is called meiosis. At fertilisation, 23 and 23 make 46 again. So half of your instructions came from a woman, in her egg cell, and half from a man, in his sperm cell. Which one of each pair goes into a sex cell is settled by chance, and the pairs also swap pieces first. This is why no two egg cells are alike, and no two sperm cells. It is also why sisters and brothers are alike in some ways and different in others.
examples: You have two copies of chromosome 1. One came from the egg cell and one from the sperm cell.
Two sisters with the same parents each got a different half from each parent.
Identical twins are the exception. They began as one zygote, which split into two embryos.
explanations.art: Two half-sets of coloured threads, one set in an egg cell and one in a sperm cell, with an arrow to a single cell holding the full set in matched pairs.

explanations.concept: Where egg cells are made, and why they are older than they look
explanations.definition: Egg cells are kept in the two ovaries. They begin to form before a girl is born, and one usually ripens and leaves an ovary each month from puberty onwards.
explanations.description: Here is a fact that surprises most adults. A girl's egg cells start forming while she is still inside her own mother. At about 20 weeks of pregnancy, her tiny ovaries hold 6 to 7 million of them. Most die back naturally. At birth 1 to 2 million are left, and at puberty about 300,000 to 400,000. Only about 400 to 500 are ever released. So think about the egg cell that became you. They were already in your mother's ovary on the day your mother was born. They waited there for all the years until you began. Why make millions and release hundreds? Nobody is sure. One idea is that the body keeps choosing among them, and only some pass. From the middle of life, at about 45 to 55, the ovaries stop releasing egg cells. This is called menopause.
examples: When your grandmother was pregnant with your mother, the egg cell that became you was already forming inside that unborn baby girl.
A woman who is 30 releases egg cells that have been waiting for a little over 30 years.
In most months only one egg cell is released. When two are released and both are fertilised, twins who are not identical can begin.

perspectives.explanation: A woman is born with all the egg cells she will ever have, and no new ones are made later.

They reported cells in adult ovaries of mice that may be able to make new egg cells. Other laboratories have not been able to show that this happens in a woman's body. The question is still argued over.

explanations.art: Three nested outlines, a grandmother, an unborn baby girl inside her, and a tiny dot inside the baby's ovary, with the dot labelled as an egg cell.

explanations.definition: Sperm cells are made in the two testes, from puberty onwards. New ones are made every day, in millions.
explanations.description: This is the opposite of the egg cell's story. A boy's testes make no sperm cells until puberty. After that they make millions every day, usually for the rest of his life. Each sperm cell takes about ten weeks to make. Why do the testes hang outside the belly, where they are easier to hurt? Sperm cells are made best about 2 degrees cooler than the inside of the body. Outside, the testes stay cooler. The finished sperm cells are stored in coiled tubes beside each testis. When they leave the body, glands add liquid that feeds and protects them. This liquid, with the sperm cells swimming in it, is called semen. It leaves through a tube in the penis. Urine uses the same tube, but never at the same moment.
examples: A sperm cell that leaves the body today began to be made about ten weeks ago.
A long, very hot bath can slow the making of sperm cells for a while, because the testes get too warm.
Elephants and whales keep their testes inside the body. Scientists are still working out how their sperm cells cope with the warmth.
explanations.art: A plain cut-away diagram of a testis showing coiled tubes inside, with tiny sperm cells at different stages along one tube.

explanations.concept: How the sperm cells reach the egg cell
explanations.definition: Sperm cells have to get from the man's body into the woman's body, and then swim to the egg tube. This can happen when two adults have sex, or with a doctor's help.
explanations.description: This card says in plain words how sperm cells reach the egg cell. A parent may want to read it first. When a grown-up woman and a grown-up man want to make a baby, they lie very close together. The man's penis goes into the woman's vagina, and semen carrying sperm cells leaves his body there. This is called sexual intercourse, or sex. It is something for adults, and only when both of them want it. The vagina is the passage that leads from the outside of a woman's body to the womb. From there the sperm cells have a long way to go. They pass through the narrow neck of the womb, across the womb, and into the egg tubes. Tens of millions or more set out. By one estimate, about 5,000 reach the openings of the egg tubes, about 1,000 enter a tube, and about 200 get near the egg cell. The woman's body does much of the sorting. Thick liquid at the neck of the womb lets through only sperm cells that swim well. Squeezes of the womb's muscle carry them along. Sperm cells can stay alive in the egg tube for a few days, waiting. Sometimes sperm cells and egg cell cannot meet this way. Then doctors can help. They can place sperm cells in the womb, or bring the cells together in a dish, which is IVF.
examples: Half the sperm cells that get across the womb enter the egg tube on the side where no egg cell was released that month.
The woman's body is not a passive road. Its muscle squeezes do much of the carrying, far faster than a sperm cell can swim.
Some couples have sex and no baby begins for many months, or ever. This is common, and it is nobody's fault.
explanations.art: A plain diagram of the womb and two egg tubes with a dotted path from the neck of the womb up into one tube, and the number of sperm cells written smaller and smaller along the path.

explanations.concept: Fertilisation: what happens when the two cells meet
explanations.definition: Fertilisation is when one sperm cell joins the egg cell and the two half-sets of chromosomes come together. The new single cell is called a zygote.
explanations.description: The egg cell is not just waiting. The egg cell and the smaller cells nearby release chemicals, and sperm cells swim towards them. The egg cell is wrapped in a clear coat. Many sperm cells reach the coat, and each one tries to work a way through. When the first one gets through and touches the egg cell, the two cells join into one. At once the egg cell changes the coat so that no other sperm cell can enter. Why does that matter? A second sperm cell would bring a third half-set of chromosomes, and the embryo could not grow properly. At this moment the egg cell also releases a burst of zinc. In 2016 scientists in the United States filmed this burst in human egg cells, using a dye that glows when it meets zinc. They named it the zinc spark. The sperm cell's tail and mitochondria are taken apart inside the egg cell. About a day later, the two half-sets of chromosomes are together, and the zygote divides into two cells.
examples: All of the zygote's working parts, and all of the mitochondria that last, came from the egg cell. The sperm cell brought half of the instructions.
The zinc spark is a real flash of zinc. It is not light that you could see with your eyes. It shows up only with a special dye and a microscope.
A pea flower does the same thing. A sperm cell from a pollen grain joins an egg cell, and that first cell grows into the baby plant inside a pea.
explanations.art: A large round egg cell joined by one sperm cell, a ring of small bright dots bursting outward from the egg cell's surface, and other sperm cells stopped at the coat.

explanations.concept: The first week: from one cell to an embryo attached in the womb
explanations.definition: In the first week the embryo divides again and again while moving along the egg tube to the womb. Then the embryo attaches to the womb's lining. This is called implantation.
explanations.description: The zygote cannot swim. Tiny waving hairs on the wall of the egg tube, and gentle squeezes of the tube, carry the embryo towards the womb. On the way, one cell becomes 2, then 4, then 8, then 16. The embryo does not get bigger in these days, because the cells get smaller each time. By about day 5 the embryo is a hollow ball of 100 to 200 cells, and has reached the womb. The ball slips out of the old egg coat. Then the embryo sticks to the soft lining of the womb and grows into it. In most pregnancies this happens 8 to 10 days after ovulation. Only now does the mother's body get the chemical message that an embryo is there. Pregnancy tests look for that chemical. Many embryos never get this far. One study in 2020 estimated that 40 to 50 in every 100 fertilised egg cells are lost before they attach. Nobody can watch this happen inside a body, so the number is an estimate. Often the embryo had the wrong number of chromosomes. The woman usually never knows.
examples: On day 3 you were about 8 cells, and still no bigger than the egg cell you began as.
Until about day 8 you were floating free. You were not yet attached to your mother.
Doctors count a pregnancy from the first day of the mother's last period. That is about two weeks before fertilisation. So '40 weeks pregnant' means the baby has been growing for about 38 weeks.
explanations.art: A row of six small pictures along an egg tube: one cell, two cells, four cells, a solid ball, a hollow ball, and the hollow ball settling into the womb lining.

explanations.concept: XX or XY: how it is settled
explanations.definition: One pair of chromosomes comes in two kinds, called X and Y. Most girls have two X chromosomes. Most boys have one X and one Y. Which it will be is settled by the sperm cell that joins the egg cell.
explanations.description: Every egg cell carries an X. Half of a man's sperm cells carry an X, and half carry a Y. If a sperm cell with an X joins the egg cell, the zygote is XX. If a sperm cell with a Y joins, the zygote is XY. Nobody chooses which sperm cell arrives. So nobody decides whether a baby is a girl or a boy. For the first weeks, XX and XY embryos look the same. At about week 6, a gene on the Y chromosome called SRY switches on. It was found in 1990. With SRY, the embryo's two small sex organs start to become testes. Without it, they become ovaries. In India some mothers have been blamed for having daughters. The science shows that this blame is wrong twice. The egg cell always brings an X. And a daughter is not a fault. Because some families wanted only sons, a law of 1994 forbids doctors in India from telling parents the sex of a baby before birth. Bodies are also more varied than two neat boxes. A small number of people have other sets, such as one X alone, or XXY. In some people the body develops in its own way between the usual patterns. And who a person knows themself to be is not read from chromosomes.
examples: A family with three daughters did not 'fail to have a son'. Three times in a row, a sperm cell with an X arrived first. Chance does that often.
Birds do it the other way round. In a hen, the egg cell carries one of two kinds of chromosome, so the mother's cell settles the sex of the chick.
In sea turtles there is no sex chromosome at all. Warmer nests in the sand hatch mostly females, and cooler nests hatch mostly males.
explanations.art: One egg cell labelled X in the middle, with two sperm cells approaching, one labelled X and one labelled Y, and two arrows to cells labelled XX and XY.

explanations.concept: Puberty: the body gets ready, years before the person is ready
explanations.definition: Puberty is the set of changes, over several years, that turn a child's body into an adult's body. The ovaries begin to release egg cells, or the testes begin to make sperm cells.
explanations.description: Puberty starts with a hormone message from a small gland under the brain. In girls it usually starts between 8 and 13. In boys it usually starts between 9 and 14. Starting early or late within that range is normal. Everyone grows faster for a while, grows hair under the arms and around the sex organs, and sweats more. In girls, breasts grow, hips widen, and periods begin. Here is what a period is. About once a month an egg cell ripens, and the womb builds a soft, thick lining with many blood vessels, ready for an embryo. If no embryo arrives, the lining is not needed. It comes away and leaves through the vagina as blood over about 3 to 7 days. Then the womb builds a new one. A period is not an illness, and the blood is not dirty. In boys, the testes and penis grow, the voice deepens, and the testes begin making sperm cells. Sometimes semen comes out during sleep. That is normal too. A body that can make a baby belongs to a person who is still a child. Being ready to raise a child comes many years later, and it is an adult's choice.
examples: A girl who has her first period at 10 and a girl who has hers at 14 are both healthy.
In some homes a girl having her period is kept out of the kitchen or the puja room. Nothing in the science supports this. Period blood is the same blood and lining that would have fed an embryo.
A boy's voice may crack for some months. His voice box is growing, and the cords in it are getting longer.
explanations.art: A circle divided into 28 small days like a clock, with five days shaded red, the next days showing a lining growing thicker, and one day in the middle marked with a small egg cell.

explanations.concept: When doctors help: IVF, and the people who were not believed
explanations.definition: In IVF, egg cells are taken from an ovary and joined with sperm cells in a dish. After a few days an embryo is placed in the womb, where the embryo may implant and grow as any other embryo does.
explanations.description: Some people cannot start a baby by having sex. The egg tubes may be blocked, there may be too few sperm cells, or the reason may be unknown. In 1944 Miriam Menkin, working in Boston with the doctor John Rock, was the first to fertilise a human egg cell in a dish. It had taken her six years of trying. In England, the scientist Robert Edwards, the nurse and embryologist Jean Purdy and the doctor Patrick Steptoe worked for ten more years. Their first IVF baby, Louise Brown, was born on 25 July 1978. Jean Purdy was the first person to see that embryo's cells dividing. Her part was left off plaques and reports for about thirty years. Just 70 days later, on 3 October 1978, a girl known as Durga was born in Kolkata. Dr Subhash Mukhopadhyay had done the work with Sunit Mukherji and Dr Saroj Kanti Bhattacharya, using simple equipment. He was not believed. A government committee dismissed his claim. He died in 1981 without credit. In 1997 another scientist, T. C. Anand Kumar, read his notes and concluded that he had truly done it. He is now credited as the maker of India's first IVF baby. Since then, millions of babies around the world have begun this way. An IVF baby grows in the womb exactly as other babies do.
examples: In IVF the zygote's first days, from one cell to a hollow ball, happen in a warm dish and not in the egg tube.
Sometimes the egg cell or the sperm cells are given by a donor, a person who helps another family to have a child.
Sometimes another woman carries the baby in her womb for the parents. She is called a surrogate.
explanations.art: A small round glass dish under a microscope, with an inset circle showing an embryo of four cells.

explanations.definition: Every person begins from one egg cell and one sperm cell. A family is the people who love and raise a child. These are two separate facts.
explanations.description: The egg cell and sperm cell tell you how a body began. They do not tell you who the family is. Some children are raised by the woman and the man whose cells they came from. Some are raised by one of them. Some are adopted, and their parents chose them by law, for life. Some live with a grandmother, an aunt and uncle, a step-parent, two mothers or two fathers, or in a big joint family where many adults share the raising. Some began with the help of IVF, a donor or a surrogate. All of these children began from an egg cell and a sperm cell, and all of these are real families. Humans have always raised children together. A human child needs care for far longer than a calf or a kitten does. One parent alone can rarely give all of it, so grandmothers, older children, neighbours and friends have always helped. Other animals raise young in many ways too. Elephant calves are looked after by aunts and older sisters. In India, adoption is arranged through a government body called the Central Adoption Resource Authority.
examples: A girl adopted as a baby has birth parents, whose cells she came from, and parents, who raise her. Both are part of her story.
A boy raised by his grandmother in Madurai while his parents work in another city has a family of three generations.
In a herd of elephants in Nagarhole, a calf is guarded and guided by several females, not only the mother.
explanations.art: Six small households drawn in a row of windows in one apartment block: a single mother and child, two fathers and a baby, grandparents with two children, a large joint family, a couple with an adopted child, and a mother, father and twins.

explanations.concept: Life is handed on: every cell comes from a living cell
explanations.definition: A cell is only ever made by a living cell dividing, or by two living cells joining. No cell in any body has been seen to form from non-living material.
explanations.description: The egg cell was alive. The sperm cell was alive. When they joined, the zygote was alive. So at no point in your beginning was there something dead that came to life. Follow it backwards. Your mother's egg cell came from cells in her body, which came from her own zygote, which came from her mother's egg cell and her father's sperm cell. In 1852 the German scientist Robert Remak showed that new cells come only from the division of existing cells. Rudolf Virchow made the idea famous in 1855, at first without giving Remak credit. If every cell comes from a cell, the line behind you goes back without a break, through people, through earlier animals, to the first cells on Earth. Those lived more than three and a half billion years ago. How those very first cells arose from chemicals that were not cells is not known. One more thread runs through this. Your mitochondria all came from the egg cell. The father's are taken apart in the early embryo. So your mitochondria came down a line of mothers only.
examples: Your mitochondria are copies of your mother's, and hers are copies of her mother's. A father cannot pass his on.
A cutting from a hibiscus plant grows into a new plant. No sex cells are involved, but the living cells are still handed on.
A bacterium has no parents in our sense. One cell divides into two, and both are the old cell continuing.
explanations.art: A long line of women standing one behind another, fading into the distance, with a thin gold thread running from each to the next and ending in a child at the front.

agreed.text: A new human begins when one sperm cell joins one egg cell, and their chromosomes come together in one cell.
agreed.evidence: In 1875 and 1876 Oscar Hertwig watched this in sea urchin eggs, which are clear enough to see into. Since 1944 it has been watched in human egg cells in a dish, and IVF depends on it.

agreed.text: Egg cells and sperm cells each carry 23 chromosomes, and other body cells carry 46.
agreed.evidence: Chromosomes can be stained and counted under a microscope. The count of 46 for human body cells was settled in 1956 by Joe Hin Tjio and Albert Levan.

agreed.text: The sex chromosomes of the zygote are settled by whether the sperm cell carries an X or a Y.
agreed.evidence: Nettie Stevens found the two kinds of sperm cell in mealworm beetles in 1905. The gene SRY on the human Y chromosome was found in 1990.

agreed.text: A girl's egg cells begin forming before she is born, and their number falls from then on.
agreed.evidence: Counts of egg cells in ovaries at different ages show 6 to 7 million at about 20 weeks of pregnancy, 1 to 2 million at birth, and far fewer by puberty.

agreed.text: The embryo attaches to the womb about 8 to 10 days after ovulation in most pregnancies.
agreed.evidence: In a study published in 1999, Allen Wilcox and co-workers tested the urine of women who were trying for a baby, every day, for the chemical an attached embryo makes.

agreed.text: Mitochondria are passed on by the mother.
agreed.evidence: The small DNA in mitochondria matches between mothers and their children, and not between fathers and their children. The sperm cell's mitochondria are destroyed in the early embryo.

challenging.context: This card is about the common picture of sperm cells racing each other to a waiting egg cell.
challenging.claim: The fastest sperm cell wins the race, and the egg cell just waits.
challenging.who: Many school books and films of the twentieth century
challenging.for: Sperm cells do swim, and only one joins the egg cell. So it looks like a race with one winner.
challenging.against: Squeezes of the womb carry sperm cells much of the way. The woman's body filters them and stores them. The egg cell releases chemicals that draw sperm cells in, and the egg cell's coat lets one through and then shuts. In 1991 the anthropologist Emily Martin showed how textbooks had told the story as a brave male and a passive female, against the evidence.

challenging.context: This card is about a very old belief that the mother settles whether a baby is a girl or a boy.
challenging.claim: The mother decides whether the baby is a girl or a boy.
challenging.who: A belief in many countries, including India, for centuries
challenging.for: The baby grows in the mother, so people assumed everything about the baby came from her body, her food or her fate.
challenging.against: Every egg cell carries an X. The sperm cell carries an X or a Y, and nobody controls which one arrives. Nettie Stevens found the two kinds of sperm cell in 1905.

challenging.context: This card is about a claim from Kolkata in 1978 that was dismissed at the time.
challenging.claim: Dr Subhash Mukhopadhyay's claim to have made India's first IVF baby in 1978 was false.
challenging.who: A committee set up by the West Bengal government in 1978
challenging.for: He worked with simple equipment, and he had not yet published full details in a journal.
challenging.against: In 1997 T. C. Anand Kumar studied his handwritten notes and concluded that the work was real. The girl, Kanupriya Agarwal, was born on 3 October 1978. India's medical research council now credits him.

challenging.context: This card is about a new idea: that an egg cell may favour some sperm cells over others.
challenging.claim: The egg cell takes part in choosing which sperm cell joins.
challenging.who: John Fitzpatrick and co-workers, in a study published in 2020
challenging.for: In the laboratory, the liquid around one woman's egg cells drew in more sperm cells from some men than from others. Which men it drew in differed from woman to woman.
challenging.against: This was measured in dishes, not inside a body, and with a small number of people. It shows attraction, but not yet that it changes which sperm cell fertilises the egg cell.

challenging.context: This card is about whether the sperm cell's mitochondria are ever passed on.
challenging.claim: A father can sometimes pass on his mitochondria.
challenging.who: Shiyu Luo and co-workers, in a study published in 2018
challenging.for: They reported three families in which some people seemed to carry mitochondrial DNA from both parents.
challenging.against: Other scientists argue that the result could come from copies of mitochondrial DNA that sit in the ordinary chromosomes. In almost all people studied, mitochondria come only from the mother.

big_questions.q: The egg cell was alive and the sperm cell was alive. So when did you begin?
big_questions.hint: Try several answers: when the egg cell formed, at fertilisation, at implantation, at the first heartbeat, at birth. What changes at each one?

big_questions.q: A different sperm cell would have made a different person. Could you have been someone else?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Two Gates Test. Which bean arrived was chance. Would that other child have been 'you'?

big_questions.q: Is a family made by cells, or by care?
big_questions.hint: Think of an adopted child, a child raised by a grandmother, and a child born through a donor. What do all their families share?

big_questions.q: Why do most animals and plants need two parents, when some living beings manage with one?
big_questions.hint: A bacterium divides. A hibiscus cutting grows. What do two parents give that one cannot? Scientists still argue about this.

big_questions.q: If nobody chooses whether a baby is a girl or a boy, is it fair to prefer one?
big_questions.hint: Use the science: which cell brings the X or the Y, and who controls which one arrives?

big_questions.q: The egg cell that became you was in your mother before she was born. How old are you, then?
big_questions.hint: Count your age from your birthday, from fertilisation, and from when the egg cell formed. Which count means the most to you?

story.title: The Egg Chaser
story.note: This story is about a real person. Miriam Menkin worked with Dr John Rock at the Free Hospital for Women in Boston from 1938. Her weekly routine, the six years without success, the night awake with her baby daughter, the three things she did differently, the two cells she saw, the lost first egg cell, the report in the journal Science in 1944 and the move to North Carolina are all recorded. Her thoughts, the words people say and the small details of the room are imagined. Nobody can be sure which of her three changes mattered most.
text: Every Tuesday for six years, Miriam Menkin went looking for something almost too small to see.

She worked in the basement of a hospital in Boston. On Tuesdays the surgeons upstairs sent down a small piece of ovary from a woman who had needed an operation. Miriam bent over it with a fine glass tube and hunted, slowly, for an egg cell. An egg cell is a speck. Find one, and you have found a grain of dust that matters.
She had a name for herself. She was the egg chaser.

Miriam had wanted to be a doctor, but in those years medical schools took very few women, and none took her. She had done all the work for a doctor's degree in science, twice, and could not pay the fee to receive it. So she was called a technician. She knew more about egg cells than almost anyone alive.

Dr Rock, upstairs, had patients who longed for a child and could not have one. In many of them the egg tubes were blocked, so the egg cell and the sperm cell could never meet. He had asked Miriam a question. Could the two cells be made to meet outside the body, in a glass dish?
Nobody had ever done it with human cells. Nobody knew if it could be done.
So Miriam had her week. On Tuesday she found an egg cell and kept the dish warm. On Wednesday she added the sperm cells. On Thursday, she said, she prayed. On Friday she looked.
And every Friday for six years, she saw one cell. One round, quiet cell, exactly as on Wednesday. Nothing had happened.
She changed the liquid in the dish. Nothing. She changed the warmth. Nothing. She kept careful notes on every egg cell, and there were a great many of them now.

The method itself she did not change, because it was the proper one. First she washed the sperm cells three times, so that they were clean. Then she put them with the egg cell for half an hour. Then she moved the egg cell to a fresh dish. Clean, quick and neat.
One week in early February 1944, Miriam did not sleep. Her baby daughter was awake and crying, hour after hour, and Miriam walked the floor with her until the windows turned grey.

That Wednesday she came to the basement with her eyes aching. She washed the sperm cells once, and was too tired to do it twice more. The sample she used was thicker than usual, crowded with sperm cells. She put them in the dish with Tuesday's egg cell and sat down at the microscope to watch.

It was something to see, even after six years. The sperm cells swarmed around the egg cell. They pushed at its clear coat from every side, so many of them that the egg cell slowly turned in the liquid.
Miriam watched, and her eyes grew heavy. When she next looked at the clock, a whole hour had gone by. Half an hour was the rule. She had left them together twice as long.
She moved the egg cell to a fresh dish, went home and slept.
On Friday morning she came down the stairs expecting what she always saw. She put the dish under the microscope and turned the wheel until the picture was sharp.
There were two cells.

She looked away and looked again. Two round cells lay side by side inside the one clear coat. The egg cell had been fertilised, and the new cell had divided. For the first time, the first day of a human being had happened in a dish, where a person could see it.
She was afraid to take her eyes off it. She sent for Dr Rock, and soon the small room was full of people taking turns at the eyepiece.

Why that week, after six years? Miriam went back through what she had done. One wash, not three. More sperm cells, crowded close. One hour, not half. She had not been careful that day. She had only been tired. But being tired had given the two cells what the proper method never had. It had given them more of each other, and more time.

A sperm cell does not slip into an egg cell in a moment. The coat is thick. Many sperm cells must work at the coat, and it takes them a long while before one gets through. For six years Miriam had been pulling the cells apart just as the work was beginning.

In the bustle, nobody photographed those first two cells, and they were lost. So Miriam did it again, on purpose this time, with one wash, a crowded sample and a full hour. Three more egg cells were fertilised. She photographed every one.
That August the report appeared in the journal Science, under two names, John Rock and Miriam Menkin.

She did not get to go on. Her husband lost his post, and the family had to move far south to North Carolina, where there was no laboratory for her and no egg cells to chase. When she came back to Boston years later, the work had moved on to other things.
Thirty-four years after that Friday morning, in 1978, a baby girl was born in England who had begun in a glass dish. Then one was born in Kolkata. Then thousands, and then millions.
Each of them began the way Miriam first saw it. Two cells that were given enough time.
story.epiphany: Fertilisation is not instant. Many sperm cells have to work at the egg cell's coat for a long time before one gets through. When the two kinds of cell were left together for longer, and more closely, they joined.
ask: For six years the careful method failed, and the tired day worked. What does that tell you about following a method?
Miriam changed three things at once that week. How could she find out which change mattered?
Why does it help a body to release so many sperm cells near one egg cell?
Miriam did the work with her own hands, and was called a technician. Who should be named when a discovery is made?
The first two cells were lost before anyone took a photograph. Why did she need to do it again?

games.title: The First Week: from the ovary to the womb
games.context: This is a board game about the first week of a new person. You start as an egg cell leaving the ovary and try to reach the lining of the womb. On the way you meet the real steps, and you find out that many tries do not get there.

printables.title: 20 spaces to draw as a winding track on a sheet of paper
items: 1. Ovary. You are a ripe egg cell. Ovulation: you leave the ovary.
2. The soft fringes of the egg tube sweep you in.
3. Tiny waving hairs on the tube wall carry you along. You cannot swim.
4. STOP. The meeting place. Roll the die. On a 1, no sperm cell reached you. Go back to space 1 as next month's egg cell. On 2 to 6, a sperm cell joins you. Fertilisation.
5. Your coat changes. No other sperm cell can get in.
6. You are a zygote: one cell with 46 chromosomes.
7. Day 1. The two half-sets of chromosomes come together.
8. STOP. You divide into 2 cells. Say where each half of your instructions came from.
9. The tube squeezes gently and moves you on.
10. Day 2. You are 4 cells. You are no bigger than before.
11. The hairs on the tube wall keep waving you along.
12. STOP. Day 3. You are 8 cells. Say why you have not grown bigger yet.
13. Day 4. You are a solid ball of 16 cells or more.
14. You leave the egg tube and enter the womb.
15. Day 5. You are a hollow ball of more than 100 cells.
16. STOP. You slip out of your old coat. Say what the coat did for you at fertilisation.
17. You float in the womb, close to the soft lining.
18. The lining is thick and ready. A hormone has kept it there.
20. STOP. Implantation. Roll the die. On a 1 or 2, you do not attach. Go back to space 1 as next month's egg cell. On 3 to 6, you attach. You have reached the end.

printables.title: Score sheet: one row for each player
items: How many times I went back to space 1
How many turns I took in all

rules: Draw a winding track of 20 spaces on a large sheet of paper. Number the spaces and copy the words for the five STOP spaces: 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20.
Each player needs a small token, such as a bean or a button. You need one die. Everyone starts on space 1.
On your turn, roll the die and move forward that many spaces. Read aloud what your space says.
You must stop on every STOP space, even if your roll would take you past. Do what the space says before your turn ends.
On space 4 and space 20 a roll can send you back to space 1. That is not losing. You start again as the next month's egg cell, and you mark it on the score sheet.
The first player to attach on space 20 wins. If you play alone, count your turns and try to finish in fewer next time.
The odds on the die are made up. In real life nobody knows the exact chances at each step.

setup.caption: 1. Draw a track of 20 spaces from the ovary to the womb lining. Colour the five STOP spaces.

setup.art: Two children and a parent sitting on the floor around the paper track, each with a bean as a token, one child rolling a die.
