setup.caption: 3. If a roll sends you back, start again as next month's egg cell and mark it down.

flow.do: 1. Draw the track of 20 spaces together. 2. Copy the words for spaces 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20. 3. Read the rules aloud. 4. Each player chooses a token.
flow.say: This track is the first week of a new person. We start as an egg cell in the ovary. Let us draw it.
flow.kid: Draw a track of 20 spaces. Write the words on the five STOP spaces. Choose a token.
flow.context: This is the first step of the game The First Week. Here you draw the board and learn the rules.
flow.parent: Keep the list of all 20 spaces beside the board, so that players can read what the plain spaces say too.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to roll and move. 2. Each player reads their space aloud. 3. On STOP spaces 8, 12 and 16, the player answers the question before the next turn. 4. Mark every return to space 1 on the score sheet.
flow.say: Read your space aloud. If it asks a question, tell us what you think before the next player rolls.
flow.kid: Roll and move. Read your space aloud. Answer the question on a STOP space. Mark it if you go back.
flow.context: This is the second step of the game The First Week. Here you play until someone attaches to the womb lining.
flow.parent: Good answers: space 8, half came from the egg cell and half from the sperm cell. Space 12, the cells get smaller each time they divide. Space 16, the coat let one sperm cell in and kept the rest out.

flow.do: 1. Count how many times each player went back to the start. 2. Ask what that part of the game stands for. 3. Ask what the game leaves out.
flow.say: How many times did we go back to the start? What do you think that stands for in a real body?
flow.kid: Count how many times you went back. What does going back stand for? What does the game leave out?
flow.context: This is the last step of the game The First Week. Here you talk about what the game shows.

ask.q: What does going back to space 1 stand for?
good: A month when no baby began.
Many egg cells are not fertilised, and many embryos do not attach.

flow.parent: In real life many months pass with no fertilisation, and an estimated 40 to 50 in 100 fertilised egg cells are lost before they attach. This is ordinary, and it is nobody's fault.

check.q: Where does a sperm cell usually join the egg cell?
check.why: Fertilisation happens in an egg tube, and the embryo then takes about five days to reach the womb. Choosing 'the womb' is common, because the womb is where the baby grows. Choosing 'the ovary' forgets that the egg cell leaves the ovary first.

games.title: True, False or Nobody Knows?
games.context: This is a card game about how a baby begins. Each card makes a claim. You say whether it is true, false or something nobody knows yet, and you give your reason.

printables.title: 22 claim cards to cut out (the claim on the front, the answer on the back)

items.f: Every person began from one egg cell and one sperm cell.
items.b: TRUE. This is so for every person, however their family was made.

items.f: The fastest sperm cell wins a race to the egg cell.
items.b: FALSE. The woman's body carries, filters and stores sperm cells, and many must work at the egg cell's coat before one gets in.

items.f: The mother's food decides whether a baby is a girl or a boy.
items.b: FALSE. Every egg cell carries an X. The sperm cell brings an X or a Y, and nobody controls which one arrives.

items.f: A baby girl is born with her egg cells already in her ovaries.
items.b: TRUE. They begin forming before she is born. About 1 to 2 million are there at birth.

items.f: A baby boy is born with all his sperm cells already made.
items.b: FALSE. The testes begin making sperm cells at puberty, and then make millions every day.

items.f: The egg cell and the sperm cell join inside the womb.
items.b: FALSE. They join in an egg tube. The embryo reaches the womb about five days later.

items.f: Period blood is dirty blood.
items.b: FALSE. It is the womb's lining, built to feed an embryo and not needed that month.

items.f: Your mitochondria came from the egg cell.
items.b: TRUE. The sperm cell's mitochondria are taken apart in the early embryo.

items.f: A baby who began by IVF grows in the womb in the same way as any other baby.
items.b: TRUE. Only the first few days happen in a dish.

items.f: An adopted child's body began in a different way from other children's.
items.b: FALSE. Every child began from an egg cell and a sperm cell. Adoption is about who raises the child.

items.f: Most babies are born on their due date.
items.b: FALSE. Only about 4 or 5 in 100 are. Most come within two weeks either side.

items.f: The embryo is attached to the womb from the first day.
items.b: FALSE. The embryo floats free for about a week, and usually attaches 8 to 10 days after ovulation.

items.f: Twins who are not identical come from two egg cells and two sperm cells.
items.b: TRUE. Two egg cells were released in the same month, and each was fertilised.

items.f: In birds, the mother's egg cell settles whether the chick is female or male.
items.b: TRUE. In birds the two kinds of sex chromosome are carried by the egg cells.

items.f: Puberty begins at the same age for everyone.
items.b: FALSE. It usually begins between 8 and 13 in girls and between 9 and 14 in boys.

items.f: A sperm cell carries 23 chromosomes.
items.b: TRUE. So does an egg cell. Together they make 46.

items.f: About half of a man's sperm cells carry an X chromosome.
items.b: TRUE. The other half carry a Y.

items.f: The egg cell helps to choose which sperm cell joins.
items.b: NOBODY KNOWS YET. A study in 2020 found that the liquid around egg cells draws in some men's sperm cells more than others. Whether this changes who is fertilised is not known.

items.f: A woman's ovaries can make new egg cells after she is born.
items.b: NOBODY KNOWS FOR SURE. Most scientists think not. A few have reported cells that might do so, and the argument goes on.

items.f: Something in the food or water of Kodinhi, in Kerala, causes the village's many twins.
items.b: NOBODY KNOWS. Kodinhi has hundreds of pairs of twins. Researchers have studied the village and have not found the cause.

items.f: The baby sends the signal that starts the birth.
items.b: NOBODY KNOWS FOR SURE. Signals from the baby, the placenta and the mother all seem to play a part. What sets the day is not understood.

items.f: Living beings have two parents because mixing instructions helps the young to resist disease.
items.b: NOBODY KNOWS FOR SURE. This is one leading idea. Scientists still argue about why two parents are so common.

rules: Cut out the 22 cards and shuffle them. Put them in a pile with the claims facing up.
On your turn, read the top claim aloud. Say 'true', 'false' or 'nobody knows', and give your reason.
Turn the card over and read the back aloud.
If your answer was right, keep the card. If your reason also matched, take an extra bean as a bonus point.
If your answer was wrong, put the card at the bottom of the pile. It will come round again.
The game ends when the pile is empty. Count one point for each card and one for each bean. If you play alone, try to beat your own score next time.

setup.art: A pile of small hand-cut paper cards on a mat with a claim written on the top card, and a small bowl of beans beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the 22 cards. Put them with the claims facing up.

setup.art: A girl holding up a card and speaking, with three fingers raised as if choosing among three answers, while her father waits to turn the card over.
setup.caption: 2. Read a claim. Say true, false or nobody knows, and say why. Then turn the card over.

flow.do: 1. Cut out and shuffle the cards. 2. Read the rules aloud. 3. Put out a bowl of beans for bonus points.
flow.say: Each card makes a claim. Some are true and some are false. For some, nobody knows yet.
flow.kid: Shuffle the cards. Some are true. Some are false. For some, nobody knows yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the game True, False or Nobody Knows. Here you set out the cards and learn the rules.
flow.parent: If you cannot print, copy the claims by hand on slips and keep the answers in a list.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read a claim and answer with a reason. 2. Turn the card over and read the back. 3. Give the card and any bonus bean. 4. Wrong cards go to the bottom of the pile.
flow.say: Read the claim. True, false or nobody knows? Give me your reason before you turn it over.
flow.kid: Read a claim. Say true, false or nobody knows. Say why. Turn it over and check.
flow.context: This is the second step of the game True, False or Nobody Knows. Here you play through the pile.
flow.parent: The reason matters more than the answer. A child who says 'false, because the egg cell always has an X' has understood more than one who guesses 'false'.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Lay out the 'nobody knows' cards together. 3. Ask which of them your child would most like to find out.
flow.say: Look at the cards where nobody knows. Which one would you most like to find the answer to? How might someone test it?
flow.kid: Count your points. Find the 'nobody knows' cards. Which would you like to find out?
flow.context: This is the last step of the game True, False or Nobody Knows. Here you look at what is still unknown.
flow.think: How can a claim be neither true nor false?
flow.parent: A claim that nobody has been able to test well enough is not false. It is open. Saying 'nobody knows yet' is a correct answer in science.

experiments.title: The Two Gates Test: if one sperm cell is enough, why do millions start?
experiments.context: In this experiment beans stand for sperm cells. Each bean must pass two gates to reach the egg cell, and a die decides who passes. You will find out how the number that start changes the chance that anyone arrives.
experiments.question: Only one sperm cell joins the egg cell. So does it matter how many start? How many must start before one usually arrives?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Each bean passes a gate only if you roll a 6, and there are two gates. If 6 beans start, will at least one arrive? What about 18 beans, or 72 beans? Write yes, no or sometimes for each group, and write the reason for your guess.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the number of beans that start. Use the same die, the same rule (only a 6 passes) and the same two gates every time. One run can be a fluke, so run the group of 6 three times and the group of 18 three times. Roll once for every bean, even when you are bored. Do not roll again for a bean you feel sorry for.
results_table: Did at least one arrive? (yes or no)

materials.item: dried beans, such as rajma, chana or groundnuts (buttons or small stones also work)
one die from a Ludo or snakes and ladders set. If you have none, write 1 to 6 on six paper chits and draw one from a tumbler each time
a large sheet of paper or newspaper, and a pen
a steel bowl or tumbler to hold the beans
a notebook, a pencil and a ruler for the table

experiments.safety: Keep dried beans away from children under three, who may put them in their mouths or noses.

schedule.what: Guess. Draw the three zones. Run 6 beans three times, 18 beans three times and 72 beans once. Fill in the table and say what the results show.

experiments.record: Fill in one row of the table for each of the seven runs. Then write three sentences: what you guessed and why, what your numbers were, and why you think so many sperm cells start.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from the Two Gates Test
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A sheet of newspaper on the floor divided by two pen lines into three zones labelled Start, Past gate 1 and At the egg cell, with a bowl of rajma beans and one die beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three zones on paper: Start, Past gate 1, At the egg cell.

setup.art: A child's hand rolling a die beside a row of beans in the Start zone, with one bean being pushed across the first line because the die shows a six.
setup.caption: 2. Roll once for each bean. Only a 6 lets that bean through the gate.

setup.art: Seventy-two beans mostly left behind in the Start zone, eleven in the middle zone, and two lone beans in the last zone beside a drawn circle labelled egg cell.
setup.caption: 3. Count how many beans reach the egg cell. Then try a different number of starters.

flow.do: 1. Read the question aloud. 2. Explain the rule: a bean passes a gate only on a 6, and there are two gates. 3. Ask for a guess for 6, 18 and 72 beans, with a reason. 4. Write the guesses down. 5. Draw the three zones and the table.
flow.say: If 6 beans start, will any reach the egg cell? What about 18, or 72? Tell me yes, no or sometimes. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess for 6 beans, 18 beans and 72 beans. Will any arrive? Say why. Draw three zones on the paper.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two Gates Test. Here you guess, and you set up the paper and the table.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say that 6 beans is plenty, because 'you only need one'. Others say more beans means a better chance, but cannot say how much better. Both are good starting points.

flow.do: 1. Put 6 beans in the Start zone. 2. Roll the die once for each bean. On a 6, move that bean past gate 1. 3. Roll once for each bean that passed. On a 6, move that bean to the egg cell. 4. Write the numbers in the table. 5. Do this run three times in all.
flow.say: Roll once for each bean. Only a 6 gets through. How many reached the egg cell this time?
flow.kid: Start 6 beans. Roll once for each. A 6 passes the gate. Do both gates. Write the numbers. Do it three times.
flow.context: This is the second step of the Two Gates Test. Here 6 beans start, three times over.
flow.parent: Most often none of the 6 arrives, in all three runs. If one does arrive, that is real chance at work. Write it down exactly as it happened.

flow.do: 1. Now start 18 beans. 2. Roll for each bean at gate 1, then for each survivor at gate 2. 3. Write the numbers. 4. Do this run three times in all. 5. Ask what your child notices so far.
flow.say: Now 18 start. Roll for every one. What do you notice so far about the small group and the bigger group?
flow.kid: Start 18 beans. Roll for each at both gates. Write the numbers. Do it three times. What do you notice?
flow.context: This is the third step of the Two Gates Test. Here 18 beans start, three times over.
flow.parent: With 18 starters, a bean arrives in roughly two runs out of five. So you may see one success in three runs, or none. Take turns rolling to keep it quick.

flow.do: 1. Start all 72 beans. 2. Roll for each one at gate 1. Line up the ones that pass. 3. Roll for each of those at gate 2. 4. Write the numbers. 5. If you have time, run 72 once more.
flow.say: Now all 72 start. This takes a while. Roll for every single bean, and keep the ones that pass in a line.
flow.kid: Start all 72 beans. Roll for every one. Line up the ones that pass. Roll again for those. Count who arrived.
flow.context: This is the fourth step of the Two Gates Test. Here 72 beans start.
flow.parent: About 12 beans usually pass gate 1, and 1 to 3 usually arrive. About one time in eight, none of the 72 arrives. If that happens, say that chance can still say no, and run it once more.

flow.do: 1. Look at the last column of the table together. 2. Ask for a claim, the evidence and a reason. 3. Only then read the explanation in the parent note together. 4. Your child writes three sentences.
flow.say: Tell me your claim, your evidence and your reason. Does the number that start matter? Why might a body send out millions?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Does the number that start matter? Say what your numbers show. Say why you think so.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Two Gates Test. Here you say and write your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.

ask.q: With 6 beans, how often did one arrive? With 72?
good: With 6, almost never.
With 72, nearly every time, but only one or two beans.

ask.q: Was the bean that arrived a special bean?
good: No. Every bean had the same chance.
The die decided, so it was chance.

ask.q: In a real body far fewer than 1 in 36 get near the egg cell. What does that tell you?
good: Then far more than 72 must start.
That is why there are millions.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: each bean had 1 chance in 36 of passing both gates. With 6 starters, usually nobody arrives. With 72, one or two usually do. So when each traveller has a small chance, many must start for one to arrive. In a real body the chance is far smaller. By one estimate only about 200 out of tens of millions get near the egg cell. The woman's body does much of the filtering, and many sperm cells swim poorly or the wrong way. Say plainly what the model leaves out. Real sperm cells are alive. They swim, sense chemicals from the egg cell and respond. Real gates are not dice. And scientists add other reasons for the huge number, which are still discussed.

check.q: In the Two Gates Test, why did a bean arrive more often when 72 started than when 6 started?
options: More starters means more chances for one to pass
The die rolls more sixes for big groups
check.why: Each bean had the same small chance, 1 in 36. With more beans there are more tries, so it is more likely that at least one gets through. Choosing 'faster' may come from picturing a race. Nothing in the test was about speed. Choosing the die means thinking chance changes with the group, but a die rolls the same way every time.

experiments.title: The Due Date Survey: does a baby arrive on the day the doctor says?
experiments.context: In this experiment you collect real numbers from people you know. A doctor gives every pregnant woman a due date, 40 weeks after her last period began. You will find out how many babies really arrive on that day.
experiments.question: Out of the births you can ask about, how many babies were born on the due date, how many before, and how many after?
experiments.predict: Guess first. If you ask about 12 births, how many of the babies came exactly on the due date? How many came early, and how many late? Write three numbers that add up to 12, and write the reason for your guess.
experiments.fair_test: Ask every person the same two questions, in the same words. Write down every answer, including the ones that surprise you. If someone is not sure, put them in a 'not sure' row and do not guess for them. Count each baby once. Note any baby that doctors delivered early on purpose, because that date was chosen and not left to the baby.
results_table: Before, on or after the due date
Was the date chosen by doctors? (yes, no, not sure)

materials.item: a notebook, a pencil and a ruler
a phone, to call or message relatives and family friends, with a grown-up's help
squared paper or plain paper for a bar chart

experiments.safety: Ask kindly, and accept 'I would rather not say'. Some births were hard, and some people do not know the story of their own birth. A grown-up chooses whom to ask.

schedule.what: Guess. Write the two questions. Draw the table. Ask the people at home.
Call or message relatives, neighbours and family friends until you have about 12 births.
Count the three groups. Draw a bar chart. Say what you found and why you think it came out that way.

experiments.record: Fill in one row for each birth. Draw a bar chart with three bars: before, on and after. Then write three sentences: what you guessed and why, what you counted, and what you think a due date really tells a family.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: 12 births compared with their due dates
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A notebook page with two questions written at the top and a four-column table ruled below, with a pencil lying across it.
setup.caption: 1. Write your two questions and draw the table.

setup.art: A girl sitting beside her grandmother on a sofa, holding a phone on speaker and writing in a notebook while the grandmother talks.
setup.caption: 2. Ask about 12 births. Write down every answer.

setup.art: A hand-drawn bar chart with three bars labelled before, on and after, the middle bar much shorter than the other two.
setup.caption: 3. Count the three groups and draw a bar for each.

flow.do: 1. Explain what a due date is. 2. Ask for a guess, with a reason, and write it down. 3. Write the two questions together. 4. Draw the table. 5. Ask the adults at home about each child they have had.
flow.say: A doctor names one day when the baby should come. Of 12 babies, how many do you think came on that exact day? Why?
flow.kid: Guess how many of 12 babies came on the due date. Say why. Write your two questions. Ask the grown-ups at home.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Due Date Survey. Here you guess, write your questions and ask the people at home.
flow.parent: The two questions can be: 'Was the baby born before, on or after the due date?' and 'By about how many days?' Many children guess that most babies come on the day. Do not correct it.

flow.do: 1. Choose relatives and friends to ask. 2. Help your child call or message them. 3. Your child asks the same two questions each time. 4. Write every answer in the table. 5. Stop at about 12 births.
flow.say: Ask the same two questions each time. Write the answer down just as they say it, even if it surprises you.
flow.kid: Call or message with a grown-up. Ask the same two questions. Write every answer. Stop at about 12 births.
flow.context: This is the second step of the Due Date Survey. Here you collect answers from relatives and friends.
flow.parent: Grandmothers often remember this very well. If you get fewer than 8 births, that is still worth counting. Just say that a small number tells you less.

flow.do: 1. Count the births before, on and after the due date. 2. Draw the bar chart. 3. Ask for a claim, the evidence and a reason. 4. Only then read the explanation in the parent note together. 5. Your child writes three sentences.
flow.say: Tell me your claim, your evidence and your reason. Do babies come on the due date? What is a due date good for, then?
flow.kid: Count the three groups. Draw the bars. Say what you found. Say why a due date might often be wrong.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Due Date Survey. Here you count, draw a chart and say what your results show.

ask.q: How many came on the exact day?
good: Very few, perhaps none or one.
Most came some days before or after.

ask.q: Why might a due date often be wrong?
good: Nobody saw the day of fertilisation.
Babies do not all take the same time to grow.

ask.q: How would births chosen by doctors change your chart?
good: Those dates were picked, so they say nothing about when the baby would have come.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: larger studies find that only about 4 or 5 babies in 100 are born on the due date. Most come within two weeks either side. A due date is counted as 40 weeks from the first day of the last period. Nobody sees the day of ovulation or of implantation, and these differ from woman to woman. Babies also differ in how long they take. So a due date is the middle of a range, not an appointment. What starts birth on a particular day is still not fully understood.

check.q: What does a due date tell a family?
options: The exact day the baby will come
The middle of the weeks when the baby is likely to come
The last day the baby can come
check.why: Only about 4 or 5 babies in 100 arrive on the due date. Most come within two weeks before or after it. Choosing 'the exact day' is the most common idea, and your own survey probably showed otherwise. Choosing 'the last day' forgets that many babies come after it.

activities.title: A Salt Grain and a Steel Plate: how small was your start?
activities.context: This is a short activity to do before anything is explained. You look at a grain of salt to picture the real size of an egg cell. Then you make the egg cell and the sperm cell two thousand times bigger, so you can compare them.

materials.item: table salt, a few grains
a sheet of dark paper or a dark cloth
a round steel plate about 20 to 25 centimetres across
one grain of raw rice and a piece of thread about 10 centimetres long
a ruler, and a magnifying glass if you have one

activities.record: Draw the plate and the rice grain with its thread tail, side by side. Under the drawing write two things you notice and one thing you wonder.

setup.art: A few grains of table salt scattered on dark paper, with a child's finger pointing at one grain and a magnifying glass held above.
setup.caption: 1. Look at one grain of salt. An egg cell is about a third as wide.

setup.art: A round steel dinner plate on a table with a single grain of rice beside it, a piece of thread laid behind the rice like a tail.
setup.caption: 2. At 2,000 times life size, the egg cell is the plate. The sperm cell is the rice grain and thread.

setup.art: A child looking from the plate to the rice grain with a puzzled face, a notebook open beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Say what you notice and what you wonder.

flow.do: 1. Sprinkle a few grains of salt on dark paper. 2. Your child picks out one grain and looks closely. 3. Say that a human egg cell is about a third as wide as that grain. 4. Say that the sperm cell is far smaller still.
flow.say: Find one grain of salt. You began as a cell about a third as wide as that. Can you picture it?
flow.kid: Look at one grain of salt. You began as a cell a third as wide. Try to picture that speck.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Salt Grain and a Steel Plate. Here you see the real size of an egg cell.
flow.parent: A grain of fine table salt is about 0.3 millimetres across. A human egg cell is about 0.1 millimetres. Salt grains vary, so this is a rough guide.

flow.do: 1. Put the steel plate on the table. Say that this is the egg cell, 2,000 times bigger. 2. Lay the thread in a wavy line and put the rice grain at one end. 3. Say that this is the sperm cell at the same scale. 4. Measure both with the ruler.
flow.say: The plate is the egg cell, made 2,000 times bigger. The rice grain with its thread tail is the sperm cell.
flow.kid: The plate is the egg cell, 2,000 times bigger. The rice and thread are the sperm cell. Measure both.
flow.context: This is the second step of A Salt Grain and a Steel Plate. Here you build both cells at the same large scale.
flow.parent: A sperm cell is about 0.05 millimetres long, so 10 centimetres at this scale. The head is about 0.005 millimetres, which becomes 1 centimetre. A grain of rice is a little short and thin for it, which is close enough.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child notices. 2. Ask what they wonder. 3. Do not explain yet. 4. Your child draws both cells and writes two noticings and one wondering.
flow.say: What do you notice about these two? What do you wonder? Why might one be so big and one so small?
flow.kid: What do you notice? What do you wonder? Why is one so big? Draw both and write your ideas.
flow.context: This is the last step of A Salt Grain and a Steel Plate. Here you say what you notice and wonder about the two cells.
flow.think: If the egg cell brings so much and the sperm cell brings so little, what does each one give?
flow.parent: Only listen. Good wonderings are: why is the egg cell so big, what is inside, how does a sperm cell find the egg cell, why the tail. The explanations answer these later.

activities.title: The Cycle Wheel: one month inside the womb and an ovary
activities.context: In this activity you make a paper wheel with 28 days on it. It shows what the womb and an ovary do in one monthly cycle, and where a period fits in.

materials.item: a sheet of thick paper or an old greeting card
a steel plate or bowl to draw round, a pencil, a ruler and scissors
red, pink and yellow crayons or colour pencils
a paper arrow and a drawing pin or a split pin, pushed in by a grown-up

activities.safety: A grown-up pushes the pin through the paper.
activities.record: Keep the wheel. On the back write one sentence for each part of the cycle: what the womb is doing and what the ovary is doing.

setup.art: A paper circle divided like a clock into 28 small numbered sections, with a pencil and ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a circle and divide the edge into 28 days.

setup.art: The same circle coloured in: days 1 to 5 red, days 6 to 13 pale pink growing darker, day 14 yellow with a small dot, days 15 to 28 deep pink.
setup.caption: 2. Colour the days: the period, the lining building, ovulation, the lining waiting.

setup.art: A child turning a paper arrow pinned to the centre of the coloured wheel so that it points at day 14.
setup.caption: 3. Pin on an arrow. Turn it and say what is happening on that day.

flow.do: 1. Draw round the plate and cut out the circle. 2. Mark 28 equal sections round the edge and number them. 3. Say that one cycle is about 28 days, but anything from 21 to 35 days is common.
flow.say: This wheel is one cycle, about a month. Day 1 is the first day of a period. Let us number 28 days.
flow.kid: Cut out a circle. Mark 28 days round the edge. Number them. Day 1 is the first day of a period.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cycle Wheel. Here you make a paper circle with 28 days on it.
flow.parent: To get 28 sections, fold the circle into quarters and mark 7 sections in each quarter. This activity is for girls and boys alike. Everyone should know how half of all bodies work.

flow.do: 1. Colour days 1 to 5 red. The old lining is leaving. 2. Colour days 6 to 13 pink. A new lining is building and an egg cell is ripening. 3. Colour day 14 yellow and draw a dot. The egg cell leaves the ovary. 4. Colour days 15 to 28 deep pink. The lining is thick and waiting.
flow.say: Before you colour each part, tell me what you think the womb is doing in those days. Then colour it.
flow.kid: Days 1 to 5 red. Days 6 to 13 pink. Day 14 yellow with a dot. Days 15 to 28 deep pink.
flow.context: This is the second step of the Cycle Wheel. Here you colour the four parts of the cycle.
flow.parent: The day numbers are for a 28-day cycle. Ovulation is about 14 days before the next period, so in a longer cycle it comes later. In the first years after periods begin, cycles are often uneven.

flow.do: 1. Pin the arrow to the centre. 2. Your child turns it to any day and says what is happening. 3. Ask what would change if an embryo arrived at about day 21. 4. Talk about how a girl can look after herself during a period.
flow.say: Turn the arrow to any day and tell me what is happening. What if an embryo arrived on day 21?
flow.kid: Turn the arrow. Say what is happening that day. What if an embryo arrived on day 21?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Cycle Wheel. Here you use the wheel to explain the cycle in your own words.

ask.q: What if an embryo arrived at about day 21?
good: The embryo would attach to the thick lining.
The lining would stay, so there would be no period.

flow.parent: If an embryo implants, the lining stays and periods stop until after the birth. This is a good moment for practical talk: pads or cloth, changing them every few hours, washing, and that cramps are common and can be eased with warmth.

check.q: What is the blood of a period?
options: Blood from a cut inside the body
The womb's lining, which was not needed this month
Dirty blood the body must get rid of
check.why: Each month the womb builds a soft lining for an embryo. If no embryo arrives, the lining comes away. Choosing 'a cut' is a natural guess, because we link blood with being hurt, but nothing is hurt. Choosing 'dirty' repeats an old belief that has no science behind it.

activities.title: Three Bowls: where were you when your grandmother was pregnant?
activities.context: In this activity you nest three bowls and a mustard seed to model a surprising fact. The egg cell that became you was already forming before your mother was born.

materials.item: steel bowls or katoris of three sizes that fit inside each other
one mustard seed
three slips of paper and a pencil

activities.record: Draw the three bowls from the side, one inside the other, with the seed in the smallest. Label them. Write one sentence about what the model shows and one about what it does not show.

setup.art: Three steel bowls of different sizes in a row with paper labels reading grandmother, mother before birth, and ovary, and a single mustard seed on a fingertip.
setup.caption: 1. Label three bowls: grandmother, mother before she was born, mother's ovary.

setup.art: The three steel bowls nested one inside another with a single mustard seed in the smallest, seen from above.
setup.caption: 2. Nest the bowls. Put the mustard seed in the smallest. The seed is the egg cell that became you.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question before showing anything. 2. Listen to the answer and the reason. 3. Label the biggest bowl 'grandmother', the middle one 'mother before she was born' and the smallest 'mother's ovary'.
flow.say: When your grandmother was pregnant with your mother, was any part of you there yet? What do you think? Why?
flow.kid: When grandmother was pregnant, was any part of you there? Say what you think. Label three bowls.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Bowls. Here you guess, and you label the bowls.
flow.parent: Most children say no. Some say 'in God's mind' or 'in the future'. Accept every answer. If your child is adopted or does not know their birth family, say 'the woman who gave birth to you' and 'her mother'. The fact is the same for everyone.

flow.do: 1. Put the middle bowl inside the biggest. 2. Put the smallest bowl inside the middle one. 3. Drop the mustard seed into the smallest. 4. Say that egg cells begin forming in a baby girl's ovaries before she is born.
flow.say: This seed is the egg cell that became you. That egg cell was forming in your mother while she was inside your grandmother.
flow.kid: Nest the bowls. Drop in the seed. The seed is the egg cell that became you.
flow.context: This is the second step of Three Bowls. Here you nest the bowls to show three generations at once.
flow.parent: At about 20 weeks of pregnancy a baby girl's ovaries hold 6 to 7 million forming egg cells. Only half of your instructions were in that egg cell. The other half came from a sperm cell made about ten weeks before you began.

flow.do: 1. Ask what the model shows well. 2. Ask what it gets wrong. 3. Your child draws and labels it.
flow.say: What does this model show well? What is not true about it? Models always leave something out.
flow.kid: What does the model show well? What is wrong with it? Draw it and label it.
flow.context: This is the last step of Three Bowls. Here you say what the model shows and what it leaves out.

ask.q: What does the model get wrong?
good: Only half of me was in the egg cell.
There were millions of egg cells, not one.
The egg cell was not 'me' yet.

flow.parent: The strongest answer is that the egg cell was not yet a person. It was one of millions, and it carried half the instructions. Leave the question of when 'you' began open.

activities.title: The Family Map: who raises a child?
activities.context: In this activity you draw a map of the people who care for you, and you read six short cards about ways a family can be made. Every person begins from an egg cell and a sperm cell, but families are made in many ways.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper and colour pencils
six slips of paper for the family cards

activities.record: Keep the map. Under it write one sentence that begins 'A family is…' in your own words.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a child's name in a circle in the middle and lines running out to other named circles of different sizes around it.
setup.caption: 1. Write your name in the middle. Draw a circle for each person who cares for you.

setup.art: Six small paper cards in a fan, each with a short handwritten line about a different kind of family.
setup.caption: 2. Read six cards about ways a family can be made.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes their name in the middle of the paper. 2. They draw a circle for each person who cares for them, near or far. 3. Beside each circle they write one thing that person does for them.
flow.say: Put yourself in the middle. Who cares for you? Draw each person, and write one thing they do for you.
flow.kid: Write your name in the middle. Draw a circle for each person who cares for you. Write what each one does.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Family Map. Here you draw the people who care for you.
flow.parent: Let your child choose who goes on the map. Grandparents, a neighbour, a teacher or an older cousin may appear. Do not correct the choices.

flow.do: 1. Write these six lines on six slips: a mother and a father who raise the child born to them. One parent raising a child. Parents who adopted their child. Grandparents raising a grandchild. Two mothers or two fathers. Parents who had help from IVF, a donor or a surrogate. 2. Your child reads each one aloud. 3. For each, ask what is the same as in the others.
flow.say: Read each card. In each family, how did the child's body begin? And who is the family?
flow.kid: Read the six cards. For each one, say how the child began. Then say who the family is.
flow.context: This is the second step of the Family Map. Here you read about six ways a family can be made.

ask.q: What is the same in all six?
good: Each child began from an egg cell and a sperm cell.
In each one, somebody loves and raises the child.

flow.parent: Use the plain words: birth parents are the people whose cells a child came from. Parents are the people who raise the child. For many children these are the same people, and for many they are not.

flow.do: 1. Ask what makes a family. 2. Listen to the answer and the reason. 3. Your child writes a sentence beginning 'A family is…' under the map.
flow.say: So what makes a family? Tell me in your own words, and tell me why you think so.
flow.kid: What makes a family? Say it in your own words. Write 'A family is…' and finish it.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Family Map. Here you put into words what a family is.
flow.think: Elephant calves are raised by aunts and sisters as well as mothers. Are they a family?
flow.parent: There is no single right sentence. Good ones mention care, time and staying.

activities.title: Carry the Bump: how does a body balance a baby in front?
activities.context: In this activity you wear a loaded school bag on your front and see what your body does to stay upright. By the end of pregnancy a woman carries several kilograms in front of her spine.

materials.item: a school bag or backpack
one-litre bottles filled with water. Each weighs about 1 kilogram
a door frame or the corner of a wall, to stand beside
a helper, a ruler and a notebook

activities.safety: Use no more than 3 bottles, and fewer for a small child. Take the bag off at once if your back hurts.
activities.record: Draw yourself from the side, twice: once with no bag and once with the bag in front. Mark where your shoulders were each time.

setup.art: A child standing side-on beside a door frame with their ankle bone level with the frame's edge, while a helper holds a ruler from the frame to the child's shoulder.
setup.caption: 1. Stand side-on by a door frame. A helper measures from the frame to your shoulder.

setup.art: The same child wearing a backpack on their front holding three water bottles, leaning back a little, with the helper measuring again.
setup.caption: 2. Wear the bag in front with 3 bottles in it. Stand as feels natural. Measure again.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands side-on to a door frame, ankle bone level with the edge. 2. They stand as feels natural. 3. The helper measures how far the shoulder is in front of or behind the edge. 4. Ask for a guess about what will change with a load in front.
flow.say: Stand how you usually stand. I will measure your shoulder. What will your body do with 3 kilograms in front? Why?
flow.kid: Stand side-on by the door frame. A helper measures your shoulder. Guess what a front load will do.
flow.context: This is the first step of Carry the Bump. Here you measure how you stand with no load.
flow.parent: The measurement is rough. Look for the direction of the change more than the exact number.

flow.do: 1. Put 3 bottles in the bag. 2. Your child wears the bag on their front and stands in the same spot for one minute. 3. Measure the shoulder again. 4. Your child walks across the room and back, and says where they feel it.
flow.say: Stand how feels comfortable now. Do not try to stand straight. Where do you feel your muscles working?
flow.kid: Wear the bag in front. Stand in the same spot. Get measured. Walk a little. Where do you feel it?
flow.context: This is the second step of Carry the Bump. Here you carry a load in front and measure how you stand.
flow.parent: Most children lean back by a few centimetres without noticing, and feel it in the lower back. If nothing changes, add time, not weight. Stand for two minutes and measure again.

flow.do: 1. Take the bag off. 2. Ask what the body did and why. 3. Then share what scientists found. 4. Your child draws the two side views.
flow.say: What did your body do? Why would leaning back help? Now imagine carrying that for months.
flow.kid: Take the bag off. What did your body do? Why? Draw yourself both ways.
flow.context: This is the last step of Carry the Bump. Here you explain why a body leans back under a front load.

good: To keep my weight over my feet.
Otherwise the load would tip me forward.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: a load in front shifts the body's balance point forward, and leaning back brings it over the feet again. In 2007 Katherine Whitcome and co-workers measured 19 pregnant women and found exactly this. They also found that the inward curve of a woman's lower back is spread over three bones of the spine, and a man's over two. They argue that this helps women carry a baby while walking upright.

activities.title: Ask, Respect, Tell: body rules and a question box
activities.context: In this activity you make a poster of three rules about bodies and touch, and a box for questions you would rather write than say. Learning how babies begin brings up questions, and every body deserves respect and privacy.

materials.item: a sheet of chart paper or the back of an old calendar, and colour pens
a small box or tin with a lid, and slips of paper

activities.record: Put the poster up where your family can see it. Keep the question box where everyone can reach it.

setup.art: A hand-made poster with three large words down the side, Ask, Respect and Tell, each with a child's drawing beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Make a poster with three rules: Ask, Respect, Tell.

setup.art: A small steel tin with a slit cut in a paper lid and folded slips of paper beside it, on a shelf.
setup.caption: 2. Make a question box. Anyone can put a question in, and a grown-up answers it honestly.

flow.do: 1. Talk through three rules. Ask before you touch someone. Respect a no, from anyone, at once. Tell a trusted grown-up if a touch or a secret feels wrong. 2. Your child writes the three words large on the poster. 3. They draw one picture for each.
flow.say: Your body belongs to you. What do you think each of these three words asks us to do? Give me an example.
flow.kid: Write three words on a poster: Ask, Respect, Tell. Draw a picture for each. Your body belongs to you.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ask, Respect, Tell. Here you make a poster of three rules about bodies and touch.
flow.parent: Use the proper names for private parts: penis, testes, vulva, vagina, breasts. A child who knows the words can tell you clearly if something is wrong. Say plainly that no adult or older child should touch their private parts or ask to see them, except to keep them clean or healthy, and that this is never a secret to keep.

flow.do: 1. Practise asking. Take turns to ask, 'May I hug you?' or 'May I sit close?' 2. The other person answers yes, no or not now. 3. Practise hearing a no without sulking. 4. Name three grown-ups your child could tell.
flow.say: Let us practise. Ask me before a hug. I might say yes, no or not now. Then we swap.
flow.kid: Practise asking, 'May I hug you?' Hear yes, no or not now. Swap. Name three grown-ups you could tell.
flow.context: This is the second step of Ask, Respect, Tell. Here you practise asking, and hearing no.
flow.parent: Say no at least once yourself, kindly, so your child sees that no is ordinary. Write the three trusted grown-ups on the poster. In India a child can also call Childline on 1098.

flow.do: 1. Cut a slit in the lid of the box. 2. Explain that anyone can post a question about bodies, growing up or babies. 3. Promise an honest answer within two days. 4. Your child writes a first question, with no name if they prefer.
flow.say: Some questions are easier to write than to say. Post any question here. I promise an honest answer.
flow.kid: Make a box with a slit. Write a question about bodies or babies. Post it. A grown-up will answer.
flow.context: This is the last step of Ask, Respect, Tell. Here you make a box for questions that are easier to write than to say.
flow.parent: If you do not know an answer, say so and find out together. A short true answer is better than a long one. You decide how much detail fits your child.

projects.title: How Our Family Came to Be: a family story book
projects.context: In this three-day project you make a small book that tells how your family came to be. It joins the science of how a body begins with the true story of the people who raise you.

materials.item: sheets of plain paper, folded in half and stapled or stitched into a book of 8 pages
pencils, colour pencils and glue
copies of family photos, if you have them and a grown-up agrees

projects.safety: A grown-up staples or stitches the book.

schedule.what: Ask the grown-ups who raise you three questions about how your family came to be. Write down what they say.
Plan eight pages. Write and draw the first four: the science of how every body begins.
Write and draw the last four pages: your own family's story. Read the book aloud to your family.

projects.record: The finished book is the record. On the back cover write the date and the names of everyone who helped to tell the story.

setup.art: A child sitting on a floor mat with a notebook, listening to a grandmother and a mother who are both talking and laughing.
setup.caption: 1. Ask the grown-ups who raise you how your family came to be.

setup.art: Four folded sheets of paper being stapled along the fold into a small book.
setup.caption: 2. Fold and fasten four sheets into a book of 8 pages.

setup.art: An open hand-made book with a drawing of an egg cell and a sperm cell on the left page and a drawing of a family at a doorway on the right page.
setup.caption: 3. Write the science first, then your family's own story.

flow.do: 1. Your child asks three questions. How did you know I was coming? Who was there to welcome me? Who has helped to raise me? 2. They write down the answers. 3. Add any story you want your child to have.
flow.say: Ask me your three questions. I will tell you the true story, and you can write down the parts you like.
flow.kid: Ask three questions about how your family came to be. Write down the answers.
flow.context: This is the first step of the family story book. Here you collect your family's true story.
flow.parent: Tell the story that is true for your family: birth, adoption, IVF, a step-parent, grandparents who raised you. If parts are painful or unknown, say so simply. A child copes better with a true short story than with a gap.

flow.do: 1. Fasten the book. 2. Your child plans eight pages. 3. Pages 1 to 4 tell the science: the egg cell, the sperm cell, fertilisation, and the first week. 4. Each page has one drawing and two sentences.
flow.say: The first four pages are true for every person on Earth. What will you put on each one?
flow.kid: Make the book. Pages 1 to 4 are the science. Draw one picture and write two sentences on each.
flow.context: This is the second step of the family story book. Here you write the pages about how every body begins.
flow.parent: Check the science gently. Each cell brings half the instructions. They join in an egg tube. The embryo attaches in the womb about a week later.

flow.do: 1. Pages 5 to 8 tell your own family's story. 2. Your child writes and draws them from the notes. 3. They read the whole book aloud to the family. 4. Everyone who helped signs the back cover.
flow.say: The last four pages belong to our family only. Read me the whole book when you have finished.
flow.kid: Pages 5 to 8 are your family's own story. Write and draw them. Read the book aloud.
flow.context: This is the last step of the family story book. Here you write your own family's pages and read the book aloud.
flow.think: Which parts of your book are true for everyone, and which are true only for you?
flow.parent: Keep the book. Children often want to add pages later, when they have new questions.

challenges.title: Move the Egg: carry a seed along a tube without touching the seed
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. An egg cell and an early embryo cannot swim. The egg tube has to move them about 10 centimetres to the womb, gently, over several days.
challenges.problem: Move one mustard seed 30 centimetres along a folded hand towel, from one end to the other, without touching the seed.
constraints: You may not touch the seed with your fingers or pick the seed up.
You may not blow on it, and you may not tilt the table or lift the towel off the table.
The seed must not be crushed or lost. If it falls off the towel, start again.
Time each design. Gentle and steady is better than fast.
materials: a hand towel folded lengthwise into a channel
a soft paintbrush or an old toothbrush
a ruler and a phone timer
general: Stroke the seed along with the soft hairs of a paintbrush, a little at a time. The egg tube is lined with tiny waving hairs called cilia that do this.
Push the towel from behind the seed with your fingers, so that a ripple travels along and carries the seed. The egg tube's muscle squeezes in waves like this.
Use both together: ripples for distance and the brush for fine control.
creative: Drum your fingertips in order under a single layer of towel, like a row of waving hairs seen from below.
Lay a few drops of water along the channel and nudge the wet seed with the brush. The real tube moves its passenger in liquid.
Sweep the comb's teeth slowly in one direction over and over. Many small strokes in the same direction act like a moving floor.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own way. Test it three times over 30 centimetres and time each run. Write which way was the gentlest, and say which part of a real egg tube your design is like.

setup.art: A hand towel folded into a long shallow channel on a table, a ruler alongside it marked to 30 centimetres, and one mustard seed at the starting end.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a towel into a channel. Put one mustard seed at one end.

setup.art: A child gently stroking a mustard seed along the towel with the hairs of a small paintbrush, another child pushing a ripple into the towel just behind.
setup.caption: 2. Move the seed 30 centimetres with no touching. Try brush strokes and ripples.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem and its limits aloud. 2. Ask how something that cannot swim could be moved along a tube. 3. Your child plans a design and says why it should work. 4. Set up the towel and the ruler.
flow.say: The embryo cannot swim. How could a soft tube move the embryo along? Tell me your plan and your reason.
flow.kid: Read the problem. How can a tube move something that cannot swim? Choose a plan. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Move the Egg. Here you plan how to move a seed with no touching.
flow.parent: Let your child try their own idea first, even if you can see a flaw. The test will show it.

flow.do: 1. Test the first design three times and time each run. 2. Try a second design and time it three times. 3. Write the times in a table. 4. Note any seed that was lost or crushed.
flow.say: Three tries for each design. Which is gentlest? Which loses the seed least often?
flow.kid: Test your design three times. Time each run. Try another design. Write the times down.
flow.context: This is the second step of Move the Egg. Here you test and time your designs.
flow.parent: Expect a run to take from 20 seconds to 2 minutes. A mustard seed rolls easily, so slow strokes work better than hard ones.

flow.do: 1. Ask which design worked best and why. 2. Then explain how a real egg tube does it. 3. Your child writes which part of the tube their design is like.
flow.say: Which design was best, and why? A real egg tube uses two of these ideas. Which two do you think?
flow.kid: Which design was best? Why? Which part of a real egg tube is it like? Write it down.
flow.context: This is the last step of Move the Egg. Here you compare your design with a real egg tube.
flow.parent: After your child has answered: the egg tube's wall has cilia, tiny hairs that wave in one direction, and muscle that squeezes in gentle waves. Both push the liquid and the embryo towards the womb. If the tube is blocked or damaged, the embryo may not get through, and that is one reason some people need IVF.

challenges.title: Explain It to a Six-Year-Old: build an honest model of how a baby begins
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about explaining. Young children ask where babies come from, and many are told things that are not true. Your task is to build a model that is simple and still correct.
challenges.problem: Build a model from things at home that shows a six-year-old how a new person begins, without saying anything false.
constraints: It must show that two cells are needed, one from each of two people.
It must show that each cell brings half of the instructions.
It must show that only one sperm cell joins, and that the first cell then divides.
You must be able to explain it in under two minutes, using no word a six-year-old does not know unless you explain that word.
materials: two colours of thread, wool or paper strips
a bowl or a ball of atta dough for the egg cell
anything else from the kitchen or the craft box
general: Use 23 short threads of one colour in the 'egg cell' bowl and 23 of another colour tied to one 'sperm cell' bean. Tip them together and count 46.
Use a ball of dough with one bean pressed in, then cut the dough in two to show the first division.
Draw it as a comic strip of four boxes: two cells, joining, one cell, two cells.
creative: Use two half-recipes on two slips of paper that only make sense when joined. Neither half can be cooked alone.
Show the coat closing: a bowl with cling film over the top, one bean pushed through a slit, and the slit then taped shut.
Act it out with family members, each holding a card for one chromosome, so that two groups of people become one group.
challenges.your_turn: Now build your own model. Try it on a real younger child, or on a grown-up pretending to be six. Write down one question they asked that your model could not answer, and how you would improve the model.

setup.art: A steel bowl holding short red threads beside a single bean with short blue threads taped on, on a kitchen table with paper and pens.
setup.caption: 1. Gather things for a model: something for the egg cell, the sperm cell and the instructions.

setup.art: An older girl kneeling on the floor showing a bowl-and-thread model to a small boy who is pointing at it and asking something.
setup.caption: 2. Explain your model to a younger child in under two minutes. Listen to their questions.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem and its four limits aloud. 2. Ask which untrue stories young children are often told. 3. Your child chooses or invents a model and says what each part stands for.
flow.say: What untrue things are little children told about babies? How could you tell it simply and truly? What will each part stand for?
flow.kid: Read the problem. Plan a model that is simple and true. Say what each part stands for.
flow.context: This is the first step of Explain It to a Six-Year-Old. Here you plan a model of how a baby begins.
flow.parent: Common untrue stories are that a bird brings the baby, that babies are bought at a hospital, or that God drops them. Your child's model does not need to mention sex. 'A cell from each of two grown-ups' is true and enough for a six-year-old.

flow.do: 1. Your child builds the model. 2. They practise the explanation once, timed. 3. Check it against the four limits together. 4. They fix anything that is missing or untrue.
flow.say: Show me, and I will time you. Then we check it against the four limits, one by one.
flow.kid: Build the model. Practise explaining it. Check the four limits. Fix what is missing.
flow.context: This is the second step of Explain It to a Six-Year-Old. Here you build the model and check it.
flow.parent: The limit most often missed is 'only one sperm cell joins'. Ask how the model shows the others being kept out.

flow.do: 1. Your child explains the model to a younger child, or to you playing a six-year-old. 2. Ask real questions a small child would ask. 3. Your child writes one question the model could not answer, and one improvement.
flow.say: I am six now. Explain it to me. I am going to ask a lot of questions.
flow.kid: Explain your model to a younger child. Listen to the questions. Write one you could not answer.
flow.context: This is the last step of Explain It to a Six-Year-Old. Here you test your model on a listener.
flow.think: Every model leaves something out. What did yours leave out, and did that make it untrue or only simpler?
flow.parent: Good questions to ask as a six-year-old: where do the two cells come from, how does the small one get there, why two and not one. A model that is simpler than the truth is fine. A model that says something false needs fixing.

items.p: Which two cells join to begin a new person?
opts: An egg cell and a sperm cell
A skin cell and a blood cell
items.why: One egg cell and one sperm cell join. Each brings half of the instructions.

items.p: The joining of a sperm cell and an egg cell is called ____.
items.why: At fertilisation the two half-sets of chromosomes come together in one cell.

items.p: How many chromosomes does a human egg cell carry?
items.why: An egg cell carries 23 and a sperm cell carries 23. Together they make the usual 46.

items.p: True or false: a baby girl is born with her egg cells already in her ovaries.
items.why: True. Egg cells begin forming before a girl is born. About 1 to 2 million are there at birth.

items.p: Where are sperm cells made?
items.why: The two testes make sperm cells from puberty onwards. The bladder only stores urine.

items.p: Match each part of the body to its work.
items.why: Egg cells ripen in an ovary and sperm cells are made in a testis. The two meet in an egg tube, and the embryo grows in the womb.

items.p: Put these in order, for the first week of a new person.
items.why: The egg cell leaves the ovary and is fertilised in the tube. The embryo divides on the way to the womb, and then attaches.

items.p: In the Two Gates Test, which starting group most often had a bean arrive?
items.why: Each bean has the same small chance. With 72 beans there are many more tries, so one usually gets through.

items.p: In the Two Gates Test, was the bean that arrived a special bean? Explain your answer.
items.a: No. Every bean had the same chance of 1 in 36. The die decided which one arrived, so it was chance.
items.why: A strong answer says that the rule was the same for every bean. Which one arrived was not about being better.

items.p: True or false: the mother's egg cell decides whether a baby is a girl or a boy.
items.why: False. Every egg cell carries an X. The sperm cell brings an X or a Y, and nobody controls which one arrives.

items.p: A sperm cell carries either an X chromosome or a ____ chromosome.
items.why: Half of a man's sperm cells carry an X and half carry a Y.

items.p: Sort each change at puberty: does it happen to girls, to boys, or to everyone?
items.why: Hormones start all of these changes. Some are shared, and some depend on whether the body has ovaries or testes.

items.p: What is a period?
opts: The womb's unused lining leaving the body
items.why: Each month the womb builds a lining for an embryo. If none arrives, the lining comes away. Nothing is injured.

items.p: Draw an egg cell and a sperm cell side by side. Label what each one brings.
items.a: A large round egg cell labelled with half the instructions, food and mitochondria. A tiny sperm cell with a tail, labelled with half the instructions.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the difference in size, and that both bring half of the instructions.

items.p: Name three different ways a family can be made.
items.a: Any three, for example: parents raising the child born to them, adoption, a single parent, grandparents raising a child, a step-family, or help from IVF.
items.why: Every child begins from an egg cell and a sperm cell. A family is the people who love and raise the child.

worksheets.title: The journey, the cycle and chance (stretch)

items.p: Why must sex cells carry half the usual number of chromosomes?
opts: So the number is 46 again after they join
So that they can swim faster
items.why: If each carried 46, the zygote would have 92, and the number would double in every generation.

items.p: True or false: the embryo gets bigger with every division in the first three days.
items.why: False. The cells get smaller each time they divide, so the embryo stays about the size of the egg cell.

items.p: After one sperm cell joins, what does the egg cell's coat do?
opts: It changes to keep other sperm cells out
items.why: A second sperm cell would bring too many chromosomes. The coat changes within moments to block it.

items.p: The embryo attaching to the lining of the womb is called ____.
items.why: Implantation usually happens 8 to 10 days after ovulation.

items.p: Put the journey of a sperm cell in order.
a: Leaves the man's body in semen
Passes the neck of the womb
items.why: Only a tiny share of the sperm cells that start get as far as the egg tube.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: the first single cell of a new person
the early stages, up to week 8
an egg cell leaves the ovary
the liquid that carries sperm cells
items.why: Each word names one step or one part of how a new person begins.

items.p: Sort each thing: does it come from the egg cell only, or from both cells?
items.why: Both cells bring half of the chromosomes. The egg cell also brings the food store and the mitochondria that last.

items.p: A family has four daughters. What is the chance that the next baby is a girl?
items.why: Each time, a sperm cell with an X or with a Y arrives by chance. Earlier babies do not change the next one.

items.p: Explain why nobody chooses whether a baby is XX or XY.
items.a: Every egg cell carries an X. Half the sperm cells carry an X and half carry a Y. Which sperm cell joins the egg cell is chance, so nobody controls it.
items.why: A strong answer names both cells and says that which sperm cell arrives is chance.

items.p: True or false: a baby who began by IVF grows in a glass dish for nine months.
items.why: False. Only the first few days happen in a dish. The embryo is then placed in the womb and grows there.

items.p: In the Due Date Survey, why must you write down answers that surprise you?
items.a: If you leave out answers you did not expect, the results only show what you already believed. A fair survey keeps every answer.
items.why: A strong answer says that choosing which answers to keep would change the result.

items.p: Draw a cycle wheel of 28 days. Shade the days of a period and mark ovulation.
items.a: A circle with 28 sections, days 1 to 5 shaded, and a mark at about day 14.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the period at the start of the cycle and ovulation near the middle.

items.p: Two girls disagree about when a person begins.

views.who: Yazhini, a girl in Class 5 (an imagined view)
views.says: A person begins at fertilisation. That is when the full set of instructions first comes together.

views.who: Ananya, a girl in Class 5 (an imagined view)
views.says: There is no single moment. The egg cell was already alive, and the embryo becomes a baby slowly.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What from this lesson supports it?
items.a: Answers vary. For Yazhini: the zygote is the first cell with this person's own set of 46 chromosomes. For Ananya: both cells were alive before, the embryo is not attached for a week, and one embryo can still split into twins.
items.why: Both girls are using the science. The facts do not settle it, because the answer depends on what we mean by 'a person'.

items.p: Why do the testes hang outside the belly?
opts: Sperm cells are made best slightly cooler
They are too large to fit inside
items.why: Sperm cells are made best about 2 degrees cooler than the inside of the body.

items.p: Chemical messages carried in the blood are called ____.
items.why: Hormones from a gland under the brain start puberty, and hormones run the monthly cycle.

worksheets.title: Testing claims about how a baby begins (challenge)

items.p: Use the Two Gates Test to explain why millions of sperm cells start.
items.a: In the test each bean had a small chance, and a bean usually arrived only when many started. In a body the chance for each sperm cell is far smaller, so far more must start for a few to arrive.
items.why: A strong answer links a small chance for each one to the need for a large number of starters.

items.p: Which of these does the Two Gates Test leave out?
opts: Real sperm cells sense and respond
items.why: Beans and a die show the part that chance plays. They cannot show living cells that swim and sense chemicals.

items.p: True or false: scientists have watched and counted embryos being lost inside a woman's body.
items.why: False. Nobody can see this happen inside a body. The figure of 40 to 50 in 100 is an estimate worked out from other measurements.

items.p: Here are two ways of telling how the sperm cell and the egg cell meet.

views.who: The race story, as many older school books told it
views.says: Sperm cells race each other. The strongest one reaches the waiting egg cell and breaks in.

views.who: Emily Martin, anthropologist, in 1991 (her argument in plain words)
views.says: The woman's body and the egg cell do much of the work. The race story came from ideas about men and women, not from the evidence.

items.ask: Which telling fits the evidence in this lesson better? Give two pieces of evidence.
items.a: Answers vary, but the evidence favours the second. The womb's squeezes carry the sperm cells, the neck of the womb filters them, the egg cell releases chemicals that attract them, and the egg cell's coat shuts after one enters.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence about what the woman's body and the egg cell actually do.

items.p: Write two scientific reasons why a mother cannot be blamed for having only daughters.
items.a: First, every egg cell carries an X, so the egg cell never settles it. Second, which sperm cell arrives is chance, so nobody controls it. A daughter is also not a fault.
items.why: A strong answer names what each cell carries and says that chance settles which sperm cell joins.

items.p: Put these in order, from longest ago, for the egg cell that became you.
a: The egg cell forms in your unborn mother
The egg cell ripens and is released
items.why: Egg cells form in a baby girl's ovaries before she is born, and wait there for many years.

items.p: Sort each claim: is it settled, or still argued about?
items: Fertilisation happens in an egg tube
Adult ovaries make new egg cells
The egg cell helps to choose the sperm cell
Why two parents are so common
items.why: Some claims have been checked many times. Others rest on a few studies that scientists still question.

items.p: Match each living being to how the sex of the young is settled.
pairs: by the sperm cell's X or Y
by a chromosome in the egg cell
by the warmth of the nest
items.why: Living beings settle this in different ways. In humans it is the sperm cell, in birds the egg cell, and in sea turtles the temperature.

items.p: Why is a hen's egg cell so much bigger than a human egg cell?
opts: All the chick's food must be packed inside
A hen's cells are always larger
items.why: A chick grows outside the mother, so the egg holds all the food. A human embryo is fed through the placenta.

items.p: A due date is 40 weeks after the last period began. Why has the baby been growing for only about 38 weeks?
items.a: Ovulation and fertilisation happen about two weeks after a period begins. So the count of 40 weeks starts about two weeks before the baby began.
items.why: A strong answer says that doctors count from the last period because that day is known, and fertilisation comes about two weeks later.

items.p: Draw three generations as three nested shapes. Show where the egg cell that became you was.
items.a: A large shape for the grandmother, a smaller one inside for the unborn mother, and a dot inside that for the egg cell.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the egg cell inside the unborn mother, who is inside the grandmother.

items.p: True or false: a cell in your body can form from material that is not alive.
items.why: False. Every cell comes from a living cell that divided, or from two living cells that joined.

items.p: Tiny waving hairs called ____ help to carry the embryo along the egg tube.
items.why: The embryo cannot swim. Cilia and gentle squeezes of the tube move the embryo towards the womb.

items.p: Is a family made by cells or by care? Give your view and one reason.
items.a: Answers vary. One view: by care, because adopted children and children raised by grandparents have real families. Another: both matter, because birth parents are part of a child's story too.
items.why: A strong answer keeps apart how a body began and who raises the child, and gives a reason.

items.p: Why would a second sperm cell entering the egg cell be a problem?
opts: The embryo would have too many chromosomes
items.why: Each sperm cell brings 23 chromosomes. Two would give the zygote 69, and the embryo could not grow properly.

quiz.p: What does a sperm cell bring to the egg cell?
opts: The food for the first week
quiz.why: The sperm cell brings 23 chromosomes, which is half. The egg cell brings the other half and the food store.

quiz.p: Where does a woman's body keep egg cells?
quiz.why: Egg cells are kept and ripened in the two ovaries. The womb is where a baby grows.

quiz.p: What does a zygote have that neither sex cell had alone?
quiz.why: The egg cell's 23 and the sperm cell's 23 make a full set of 46 in the zygote.

quiz.p: Where do the egg cell and the sperm cell usually meet?
quiz.why: They meet in an egg tube. The embryo reaches the womb about five days later.

quiz.p: About when does the embryo attach to the lining of the womb?
quiz.why: The embryo floats free for about a week and then attaches. This is implantation.

quiz.p: Each traveller has only a small chance of arriving. What makes it likely that one arrives?
quiz.why: In the Two Gates Test a bean usually arrived only when many started. More starters means more chances.

quiz.p: Which cell settles whether the zygote is XX or XY?
opts: Neither. It is settled at birth
quiz.why: Every egg cell carries an X. The sperm cell carries an X or a Y.

quiz.p: What starts the changes of puberty?
opts: Hormone messages from a gland under the brain
quiz.why: A small gland under the brain sends hormones to the ovaries or testes. The age differs from child to child.

quiz.p: If no embryo arrives in a month, what happens to the womb's lining?
opts: It comes away as a period
It stays for the next month
It turns into an egg cell
quiz.why: The lining is not needed, so it comes away and leaves as a period. Then a new lining is built.

quiz.p: What is the same about a child born after IVF and every other child?
opts: Both began from an egg cell and a sperm cell
Both began in a glass dish
quiz.why: Every person begins from one egg cell and one sperm cell. In IVF the two cells meet in a dish.

quiz.p: Who are an adopted child's parents?
opts: The people who raise the child
quiz.why: Adoption makes the people who raise a child their parents, by law and for life. Birth parents are part of the child's story too.

quiz.p: Why can scientists only estimate how many embryos are lost before they attach?
opts: Nobody can see it happen inside a body
Nobody has tried to find out
It happens only in other animals
quiz.why: The embryo is tiny and hidden, and the woman usually does not know. So the number is worked out from other measurements.

applications: Fertility doctors use the timing of ovulation and the short life of the egg cell to help couples who want a baby.
IVF brings egg cells and sperm cells together in a dish. It has helped millions of families who could not have a child otherwise.
Pregnancy tests look for a chemical that an embryo makes only after attaching to the womb.
Families use the knowledge of ovulation and fertilisation to choose when to have children, and how many.
Schools and health workers teach about periods, so that no girl is frightened by her first one or kept away from school.
Farmers and wildlife breeders use the same science. Many dairy calves in India begin when a vet places sperm cells in a cow's womb.
Courts and adoption agencies keep apart two questions that science also keeps apart: whose cells a child came from, and who the child's parents are.

open_questions.q: What sets the day a baby is born?
open_questions.why_open: Signals from the baby, the placenta and the mother all seem to take part. Nobody can yet say what starts birth on one day and not another. This is why due dates are so often wrong, and why doctors cannot yet prevent most early births.

open_questions.q: Why are so many embryos lost in the first week?
open_questions.why_open: Many have the wrong number of chromosomes, but that does not explain all of the losses. The losses happen where nobody can see them, so even the number is an estimate.

open_questions.q: Does the egg cell take part in choosing the sperm cell?
open_questions.why_open: Laboratory studies show that the liquid around egg cells attracts some men's sperm cells more than others. Nobody has shown what this does inside a body.

open_questions.q: Why do most animals and plants have two parents at all?
open_questions.why_open: A living being who simply copies themself passes on all of their instructions, not half. So two parents look costly. The leading ideas are that mixing helps the young resist disease and clears out harmful changes in the DNA. None has been shown to be the whole answer.

open_questions.q: Why are there so many twins in Kodinhi?
open_questions.why_open: The village in Kerala has several times as many twins as the rest of India. Researchers have looked at food, water and family histories, and have not found a cause.

open_questions.q: How did the first cells arise, if every cell comes from a cell?
open_questions.why_open: The line of living cells must have had a first link, more than three and a half billion years ago. Chemists can make some of the building blocks of cells, but nobody has made a living cell from non-living material.

ask_kids: Where was the egg cell that became you on the day your mother was born?
If only one sperm cell is needed, why do millions set out?
Which do you think does more of the work of meeting, the egg cell or the sperm cell? Why?
A family has three sons. What is the chance the next baby is a son?
Why do you think the embryo does not grow bigger in the first three days?
Who are all the people who have helped to raise you?
Why is a hen's egg so big when a human egg cell is a speck?
What is one thing about how babies begin that nobody knows yet?

jokes.j: What did the zygote say after the first day?
Why did the embryo do so well in maths?
What did one identical twin embryo say to the other?
Why don't your mitochondria take after your father?
What do you call a due date that turns out right?
How does an embryo travel to the womb?
jokes.a: First class. Carried all the way, and no swimming.

jokes.j: Why did the sperm cell cross the womb?
jokes.a: To get to the other tube. Wrong tube again.
