maths.problem: In the Two Gates Test a bean passes each gate only on a 6. What fraction of beans should pass both gates? If 72 start, how many should arrive, on average?
maths.answer: 1 in 36 should pass both gates. Of 72 beans, 2 should arrive on average.
maths.explain: A 6 comes up 1 time in 6. Passing two gates needs two sixes: 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36. 72 ÷ 36 = 2. In any one run you may get 0, 1, 2, 3 or more, because chance varies.
maths.context: In the Two Gates Test you rolled a die for each bean at two gates, and counted how many reached the egg cell.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the two chances tells you what to expect before you roll, so you can compare your real results with it.

maths.problem: Suppose 200,000,000 sperm cells start and 200 get near the egg cell. What fraction get near? Compare it with 1 in 36 from the Two Gates Test.
maths.answer: 1 in 1,000,000 get near the egg cell. That is far smaller than 1 in 36.
maths.explain: 200,000,000 ÷ 200 = 1,000,000. So one in a million gets near. A chance of 1 in 36 needed about 72 starters. A chance of one in a million needs millions of starters.
maths.context: In the Two Gates Test a bean usually arrived only when many started. Real numbers are far larger. These are rounded estimates.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the starters by the arrivals shows how small the real chance is, and so why the real number of starters is so large.

maths.problem: A salt grain is about 0.3 millimetres wide, and an egg cell about 0.1 millimetres. At 2,000 times life size, how wide is each? How tall would a child of 130 centimetres be?
maths.answer: The egg cell is 20 centimetres wide and the salt grain 60 centimetres. The child would be 2.6 kilometres tall.
maths.context: In A Salt Grain and a Steel Plate you used a plate for an egg cell made 2,000 times bigger.
maths.why_maths: Scaling everything by the same number lets you compare sizes that are too small to see with sizes you know.

maths.problem: A girl has about 1,000,000 egg cells at birth. About 400 are released in her life. What fraction is released? Write it as 1 in something.
maths.explain: 1,000,000 ÷ 400 = 2,500. So for every egg cell released, about 2,499 are not.
maths.context: In Three Bowls one mustard seed stood for the egg cell that became you. In a real ovary there were about a million.
maths.why_maths: Writing the numbers as a ratio shows how unlikely it was for any one egg cell to be the one released.

maths.problem: A cycle is about 28 days. A woman has cycles from about age 13 to age 50. About how many cycles is that? Why might the real number be lower?
maths.answer: About 480 cycles. The real number is often lower, because cycles stop during pregnancy and often during breastfeeding.
maths.explain: 365 ÷ 28 is about 13 cycles a year. 50 − 13 = 37 years. 37 × 13 = 481. This is close to the 400 to 500 egg cells released in a lifetime.
maths.context: In the Cycle Wheel you made a wheel of one 28-day cycle, with one ovulation in it.
maths.why_maths: Counting the cycles in a lifetime explains where the figure of 400 to 500 released egg cells comes from.

maths.problem: In a made-up Due Date Survey of 20 births, 1 baby came on the due date, 11 before and 8 after. What percentage came on the date? Is this close to what large studies find?
maths.answer: 5 percent came on the due date. Large studies find about 4 or 5 percent, so it is close.
maths.explain: 1 out of 20 is 1 ÷ 20 = 0.05, which is 5 percent. With only 20 births, one more or one fewer would change the answer a lot, so a small survey gives only a rough figure.
maths.context: In the Due Date Survey you asked people whether babies came before, on or after the due date.

maths.why_maths: A percentage lets you compare your small survey with studies of many thousands of births.

how_we_found_out.context: For most of history nobody knew what a man and a woman each give to start a baby. This is how people found out.
how_we_found_out.story: For centuries many scholars thought only one parent gave the baby. Some said a tiny person lay ready in the egg. Others said it lay in the semen, and the mother was only the soil. In 1677 Antonie van Leeuwenhoek saw sperm cells with his microscope. Most people decided they were tiny worms living in the liquid. In the 1760s the Italian priest and scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani tested it. He dressed male frogs in tight little trousers of waxed silk. The eggs of their mates did not grow. When he painted those eggs with the liquid caught in the trousers, tadpoles grew. So the liquid had to touch the egg. He also found that filtered liquid did nothing. Even so, he went on thinking the 'worms' did not matter. In 1827 Karl Ernst von Baer found the egg cell of a mammal, in a dog. In 1875 Oscar Hertwig watched sea urchin eggs, which are clear like glass. He saw one sperm cell enter, and saw the nucleus inside join the egg's nucleus. Both parents give half.
how_we_found_out.who: Lazzaro Spallanzani, Karl Ernst von Baer and Oscar Hertwig. Hermann Fol saw a sperm cell enter an egg cell at about the same time as Hertwig.
how_we_found_out.when: Spallanzani's frog tests were done in the 1760s and later. Von Baer reported the mammal egg cell in 1827. Hertwig's work was done in 1875 and published in 1876.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That only one parent gives the baby, either as a ready-made tiny person in the egg or as a seed in the semen, and that sperm cells are only worms living in the liquid. Spallanzani's own filter test pointed against this, and Hertwig then saw one sperm cell's nucleus join the egg cell's nucleus.
how_we_found_out.art: An eighteenth-century scientist at a wooden table gently holding a frog who is wearing tiny pale silk trousers, with a bowl of frog eggs beside him.

roots.context: We have learned how an egg cell and a sperm cell join to begin a new person. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Two Gates Test you asked which sperm cell arrives. But that sperm cell and the egg cell were both alive before they met. The egg cell was alive in your mother before she was born. So no life started when you started. A new person began, and life carried on.
deep_truth.habit: We say a baby is 'the start of a new life', as if something that was not alive got switched on. But nothing was switched on. Two living cells became one living cell. What is new is the person, and the word 'beginning' hides how much was already there.
deep_truth.evidence: The egg cell that became you formed in your mother's ovary before her birth. Remak showed in 1852 that cells come only from living cells. Nobody has seen a cell in a body form from non-living material. Your mitochondria came unbroken down a line of mothers.

three.who_am_i: You are a new person. But the living cells you are made of have never once been dead. They were handed to you, and they were handed to the people before you.
three.what_is_life: Life in a body is not made fresh each time. Living cells pass it on by dividing and joining. Each of those cells senses the world and responds to it.
three.what_is_this_world: The world has been making living bodies without a break for more than three and a half billion years. You are where that long making has reached today.

roots.thread: Before the first cells there was a world with no cells in it. How the first living cells arose is not known. Since then, one unbroken stream of living cells has divided, joined and divided again. Out of that one stream came every bacterium, banyan, crow and person. You look like a separate thing with a start date. Seen from the cells, you are the same stream, in a new and never-repeated shape. The sperm cell and the egg cell each sensed the other and moved to join. That reaching towards another is as old as cells.

teachings.teaching: The spirit of the valley never dies. It is called the mysterious female. Her gateway is the root of heaven and earth. It goes on and on, and using it never wears it out.
teachings.link: Laozi pictured the source of everything as a mother who never stops giving birth. The science of this lesson found something close to it in every body: a line of living cells, and of mothers, that has not stopped.
verse: 谷神不死，是謂玄牝。玄牝之門，是謂天地根。緜緜若存，用之不勤。

teachings.teaching: King Milinda asks whether a person stays the same from baby to adult. The monk Nagasena asks about a lamp that burns all night. The flame of the first hours and the flame of the last hours are neither the same flame nor a different one.
teachings.link: A zygote, a baby and you are like that flame. Go further back, and the flame was never lit from nothing. A living cell was lit from a living cell.

teachings.teaching: Your children are not your children. They are the sons and daughters of Life's longing for itself. They come through you but not from you.
teachings.link: Parents do not build a child out of nothing. Life passes through them, in two cells, and becomes someone new who belongs to themself.

science.text: Every cell comes from a living cell. No cell in a body has been seen to form from non-living material.
The first cells on Earth arose from chemistry that was not yet cells, more than three and a half billion years ago. How this happened is not known.
Science can describe each step from egg cell to baby. It cannot say on its own at which step 'a person' begins, because that depends on what we mean by a person.

other_view.who: Many religious traditions, in different ways
other_view.view: Many traditions teach that each person does have a true beginning: a soul that enters the body at a certain moment. Some place it at fertilisation, some weeks later, and some at the first breath. On this view the cells are only the house, and the one who lives in it arrives new. Science cannot measure a soul, so it cannot settle this.

practice.title: The line behind you
practice.say: Sit still and put one hand on your belly button. Breathe slowly three times. Your belly button is where you were joined to your mother. Now picture her as a baby, joined to her mother. Picture that grandmother as a baby, joined to her mother. Go back as far as you can. Every one of them was alive. Now come forward again to your own breath. What does it feel like to be at the front of that line?
practice.kid: Sit still. Put a hand on your belly button. Breathe slowly three times. Picture your mother as a baby. Picture her mother as a baby. Go back as far as you can. Then come back to your own breath.

ask: If life was handed to you and not started in you, what exactly began on the day you began?
Is the flame of a lamp at midnight the same flame as at dawn? Are you the same one who was a zygote?
Some people say a person begins at one exact moment. Some say it happens slowly. What do you think, and what makes you think so?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game and challenge in this lesson was reasoned through step by step as a family in a city flat would do it. None has yet been tried at home, so please treat times as a starting point. A parent should read the explanation 'How the sperm cells reach the egg cell' and the card on puberty before the child does, and decide how much to add. The Two Gates Test (in the core path) needs 72 beans and one die. The chances were worked out exactly: with 6 starters a bean arrives in about one run in six, with 18 in about two runs in five, and with 72 in about seven runs in eight. So a family will sometimes see 72 beans fail, and the parent note says what to do. Rolling for all seven runs is about 170 rolls and takes about 15 minutes if two people share it. The Due Date Survey depends on relatives remembering. Eight births are enough to see the pattern, and births whose date was chosen by doctors should be marked. In A Salt Grain and a Steel Plate, salt grains vary in size, so the comparison is rough. In Carry the Bump the measurement is rough too, and the lean is small. Look for the direction of the change, and use no more than 3 kilograms. In Move the Egg a mustard seed rolls easily, so slow strokes work best. The Cycle Wheel uses a 28-day cycle as an example, and real cycles vary. The Family Map, Three Bowls and the family story book are written so that adopted children and children who do not know their birth families can do them fully. The board game The First Week was read through for one, two and three players. Its odds are made up and the rules say so. Facts checked against published sources while writing: the counts of egg cells at 20 weeks, at birth and at puberty, the length of a sperm cell and the size of an egg cell, the estimate of how many sperm cells reach the egg tube, the timing of implantation, the estimate of early embryo loss, the zinc spark study of 2016, the 2020 study of egg cells attracting sperm cells, Miriam Menkin's 1944 experiment, the births of Louise Brown and of Durga in 1978 and the later recognition of Subhash Mukhopadhyay, Jean Purdy's part, the discovery of the SRY gene in 1990, the 1994 law in India on telling a baby's sex, the usual ages of puberty, how mitochondria are inherited, the twins of Kodinhi, the 2007 study of pregnant women's spines, Remak and Virchow, the frog experiments of Spallanzani and Hertwig's sea urchin work, the 1956 chromosome count, and the share of babies born on the due date. Not checked afresh and taken from standard textbooks: that an egg cell lives about a day after ovulation, sex chromosomes in birds, nest temperature in sea turtles, Nettie Stevens's work of 1905, and the Childline number 1098. The titles and channels of the three videos were confirmed through YouTube's public lookup, but the videos were not watched.
